TI Large language models for generating key-feature questions in medical
   education
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE ChatGPT; large language models; key-feature questions; key-feature
   problems; medical education; cardiology
AB In this study, we conducted a descriptive study to evaluate the quality of KFQs generated by OpenAI's o3 model. We developed a reusable generic prompt for KFQ generation, designed in alignment with the Medical Council of Canada's KFQ development guidelines. We also created an evaluation metric to systematically assess the quality of the KFQs based on the KFQ development guideline. Twenty unique cardiology-focused KFQs were created using recent European Society of Cardiology guidelines as reference. Each KFQ was independently assessed by two cardiology experts using the quality checklist, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize checklist compliance and final acceptability ratings. Of the 20 KFQs, 3 (15%) were rated 'Accept as is' and 17 (85%) 'Accept with minor revisions'; none required major revisions or were rejected. The overall compliance rate across checklist criteria was 93.7%, with perfect scores in domains such as key feature definition, scenario plausibility, and alignment between questions and scenarios. Lower performance was observed for inclusion of genuinely harmful 'killer' responses (50%), plausibility of distractors (77.8%), and active language use in phrasing the question (80%). The findings showed that an LLM, guided by a structured prompt, can generate KFQs that closely adhere to established quality standards, with most requiring only minor refinements. While expert review remains essential to ensure clinical accuracy and patient safety, AI-assisted workflows have strong potential to streamline KFQ development and enhance the scalability of CDM assessment in medical education.

TI How cultural factors affect medical students' interactions with clinical
   practice feedback: a qualitative study of ethnically diverse students at
   three transcontinental campuses
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Feedback; learning culture; cultural diversity; international medical
   graduates; feedback literacy
ID LEARNING CULTURE; GLOBALIZATION; PERCEPTIONS; IDENTITY; SATURATION;
   INTERVIEWS; RESIDENTS; EMOTIONS; IMPACT; MODEL
AB Transnational medical educational programs are now commonplace. Given the importance of individualised feedback, this study explored how cultural factors influence feedback experiences across three transnational campuses of one medical school. A total of 57 final-year medical students were interviewed from a sampling frame of 514 (269 male, 245 female). One-to-one semi-structured interviews were conducted and analysed using template analysis. Codes were iteratively refined into four themes, which were critically reviewed through the lenses of Hofstede's cultural dimensions and Figured Worlds. Four themes were identified: (1) early socialisation into feedback shaped by family and schooling; (2) hierarchical learning environments positioning students as passive recipients; (3) strategies to cope with negative feedback; and (4) gendered differences in the interpretation of feedback. National identity played only a minor role, while prior experiences and hierarchical structures were more influential. Female students more often described humiliation and emotional burden, whereas some male students framed negative feedback as a 'rite of passage.' Feedback experiences in transnational medical programs appear less determined by national culture than by early life experiences and hierarchical clinical environments. Hofstede's framework offered limited explanatory value, while Figured Worlds illuminated how identities are negotiated in feedback encounters. To enhance feedback cultures in transnational settings, faculty development should prioritise dialogic approaches, sensitivity to learners' prior experiences, and awareness of gendered impacts. Institutional change is needed to move beyond transmissive practices and foster learner-centred, inclusive feedback.

TI Gender difference as protective and risk factors in the Competence
   for Living in Equality (CLE) in adolescents
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Competence for Living in Equality (CLE); psychological protective and
   risk factors; bio-psycho-social model; gender differences; secondary
   education; Educational Psychology; Positive Psychology; School
   Psychology; Primary and Secondary Prevention
AB Competence for Living in Equality (CLE) has generally been seen as a protective adjustment factor that mitigates the impact of risk factors on living together. The aim of this research was: (1) to ascertain the level of equality competencies that are present in students of compulsory secondary education, (2) to analyze the multicausal predictive value of gender. It was hypothesized that male students would have lower levels of CLE. The sample was formed by 3665 students in compulsory secondary education (7th to 10th grades), with balanced distribution by year-in-school and sex. A validated short form of the CLE Scale was used. Using an ex post facto design, we carried out descriptive, association, and linear prediction analyses. Results support the existence of risk factors and protective factors in relation to CLE. Moreover, gender differences were observed in these factors, with significantly higher scores for sexism in the male students, and for protective factors in the female students. These results highlight the importance of an essential, coordinated effort between schools, families and society to create formal, nonformal and informal educational contexts to address living in equality.

TI Stress level of Islamic junior and senior high school students in
   distance learning during the COVID-19 outbreak
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Distance learning; stress; psychological difficulties; COVID-19
ID CONVENIENCE; IMPACT
AB The COVID-19 pandemic impacted education, as indicated by the transition from face-to-face to distance learning, which is perceived to influence students' stress. This study aims to measure the psychological condition of students in Indonesia based on their stress levels. It used a quantitative approach with 1,174 students at Islamic junior and senior high schools in Bali and Nusa Tenggara Timur as respondents. They were selected through a convenience sampling technique. Data were collected through online questionnaires distributed from 9 to 26 November 2021, and two main findings were discovered. First, students' stress levels were in the 'moderate' category, with 13,29% experiencing high-stress levels and 41,82% at moderate levels. Second, students reported physical, emotional, and behavioural difficulties with some stressors such as fatigue, headaches, irritability, anxiety, decreased learning motivation, and concentration. These findings enrich the discourse about distance learning, which previously stressed its negative impact more. The findings recommend that educational institutions provide students with innovative and diverse models of enjoyable distance learning that do not result in psychological problems for them.

TI 'The often-forgotten middle child': Student transitions and engagement
   through higher education
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Through-university transitions; student engagement; second-year
   undergraduates; student wellbeing; higher education
ID RECOMMENDATIONS
AB This paper reports on a mixed methods study exploring the views and experiences of second year undergraduate students in Wales as they continue their academic journey through HE. Our findings build on previous research exploring first year student transitions and engagement and provides a unique insight into second year student engagement. Findings include the importance of peer support, a demand for increased face-to-face teaching and a need for a more robust re-induction process. We recognise that undergraduates now live more complex lives, often juggling study with work and/or caring responsibilities, which requires effective planning at institutional and programme level (i.e. early timetable release). To better support second year undergraduates, we recommend that institutions also focus on providing support services to students, and that academic staff signpost appropriate support during academic sessions and as part of the personal tutoring process. Finally, we recommend that students engage in physical activity and have conversations with their peers to help manage their wellbeing. The paper considers implications for institutional policy and programme development and recognises the need for further research on induction and re-induction practices and their impact on student engagement and outcomes.

TI Terra incognita: exploring Ukrainian pre-service EFL teachers'
   cognitions
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Longitudinal study; narrative inquiry; pre-service EFL teachers; teacher
   cognition; sociocultural theory; Ukraine
ID BELIEFS; IDENTITY; ENGLAND
AB In becoming English as a Foreign Language (EFL) professionals, teachers typically pass through three key developmental stages-school language learning experiences, teacher training programs, and teaching practicum-which shape their cognitions in terms of what they know, believe, and think as EFL teachers. Addressing a significant knowledge gap in the Ukrainian EFL context, the current longitudinal study examined the formation of language teacher cognitions among Ukrainian pre-service EFL teachers to make a worthwhile contribution to the national EFL teaching knowledge base. Data were collected from 24 participants through semi-structured interviews following a narrative inquiry approach. The results reveal that secondary school teachers' professional competence and adequacy of language practice activities are major factors underpinning the formation of pre-service teachers' cognitions. A negative school imprint can trigger critical reflection, fostering a positive mindset and commitment to the profession. The findings indicate that pre-service education courses at teacher training institutions inform pre-service teachers' understanding of desirable teacher attributes, as they value the knowledge acquired through these programs despite the apparent impracticality of some of the courses. Pre-service teachers also value the teaching practicum for providing opportunities for self-reflection, professional growth, and mentorship, supporting their development as proficient teachers.

TI The educational, physical and social dimensions of school loneliness:
   staff insights from Swedish schools
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE School loneliness; school belonging; staff perspectives; educational
   environment; social inclusion; Teachers & Teacher Education; Childhood;
   Classroom Practice; Inclusion and Special Educational Needs; School
   Leadership, Management & Administration; Sociology of Education
ID ADOLESCENTS
AB The aim of this study was to explore student loneliness and a lack of sense of belonging in Swedish schools, and to gain insight from school staff on how to identify and address these issues. Fourteen school personnel-including counsellors, special educators, and teachers-were interviewed using a semi-structured approach. The data were analysed thematically, both inductively and deductively. According to the staff, loneliness and lack of belonging are widespread phenomena, observable throughout the school day-for example, during breaks and other social interactions. These are complex phenomena influenced by both individual and environmental factors. Contributing elements to students' school experiences were identified within the educational, physical, and social aspects of schooling. In particular staff highlighted how these aspects intertwine and may negatively affect students' feelings of isolation and alienation. Key implications include the need for school leaders and policy makers to consider the interconnectedness of these dimensions-the educational, physical, and social aspects of schooling-in order to effectively address loneliness and foster more inclusive and supportive school environments for all students.

TI A Heart-Mind Model for developing multidimensional thinking among
   mathematics teacher students: a quasi-experimental approach
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Heart-Mind Model; cognitive thinking; emotional thinking; practical
   thinking; multidimensional thinking
ID BRAIN; PERFORMANCE; POTENTIALS; EMOTION
AB This study aimed to experimentally verify the effectiveness of the Heart-Mind Model in developing multidimensional thinking among mathematics teacher students in universities. The study employed a quasi-experimental approach to examine the relationships between different dimensions of thinking and the impact of teaching using the Heart-Mind Model on multidimensional thinking. A multidimensional thinking test was applied, consisting of a cognitive thinking test, an emotional thinking scale and a practical performance test. The sample included 60 students from the Faculty of Education at Dhamar University, Yemen. The study's findings revealed that cognitive thinking was positively correlated with both emotional and practical thinking. Similarly, a positive correlation was found between emotional and practical thinking. The results indicate that instruction using the Heart-Mind Model was associated with higher post-test scores; however, causal interpretation should be cautious. This model may be associated with improvements in multidimensional thinking within the present sample; further studies are needed to assess generalizability.

TI Students' engagement with teacher oral corrective feedback: insights
   from an Ethiopian EFL classroom
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Student engagement; teacher oral corrective feedback; EFL classroom;
   case study; oral feedback types
ID BELIEFS
AB This instrumental case study explored students' engagement with teacher oral corrective feedback in an EFL classroom at Bahir Dar University, Ethiopia. The study aimed to shed light on the complex nature of oral corrective practices and students' reactions to the feedback. For this qualitative case study, the data were collected through audio-recorded classroom observation and student interview questions. After these data were transcribed, they were thematically analyzed. The results of the study unveiled the teacher's application of recast as a major feedback strategy in the EFL classroom, and the teacher predominantly deployed immediate feedback. The findings of this study contribute to the existing body of literature in the field of student engagement with oral corrective feedback. Again, the findings can inform English language teachers to fit their oral correction strategies to students' needs and emotional well-being in EFL classrooms.

TI Challenging assumptions in ELT: a sequential explanatory study on the
   impact of 'native-speakerism' on perceived professionalism
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Native speaking teacher; nonnative speaking teacher; MGE;
   professionalism; CDA
ID LANGUAGE PROFICIENCY; ENGLISH; TEACHERS; BELIEFS; ATTITUDES; EFFICACY
AB Many practices in English Language Teaching (ELT) appear to be grounded in intuitive knowledge rather than scientific evidence. The concept of the 'native-like speaker' has gained widespread acceptance as a common assumption in educational institutions, including schools, universities, language centres, and teacher training programs. This study investigates the conscious and/or unconscious adoption, usage, and promotion of the 'native-like speaking teacher'. To test the hypothesis that English teachers are more favourably perceived when they speak with a native-like accent compared to a localized Moroccan accent, a sequential explanatory study was employed, integrating quantitative and qualitative data analysis techniques. The quantitative component involves a Matched Guise Experiment to assess respondents' biases toward Moroccan Accented English Teachers (MAETs) and Native Accented English Teachers (NAETs). The qualitative aspect employs Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) based on Teun Van Dijk's framework to examine an American Language Centre's online job advertisement and a teacher description passage. The findings indicate a discernible pattern wherein the 'native-like speaking teacher', despite its pseudo-scientific nature, is used in a discriminatory manner as a benchmark not only for assessing Moroccan teachers' English language proficiency but also for evaluating their teaching effectiveness and professionalism. The results highlight the need for a more evidence-based approach to ELT principles and emphasize the importance of critically examining assumptions ingrained in teaching principles and methodologies.

TI A holistic exploration of student attitudes toward AI use in higher
   education: an international comparison
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI; student attitudes; prevalence of use; pros and cons; ethical
   concerns; Social Sciences; Behavioral Sciences; Work & Organizational
   Psychology; Industrial/Organization Psychology Tests and Assessments;
   Leadership
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; TECHNOLOGY; ACCEPTANCE; CHATBOTS; CULTURE
AB This study investigates higher education students' perspectives on artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and their use in learning and academic contexts. As AI increasingly influences higher education, understanding students' attitudes and ethical awareness is essential. The research involved 920 students from higher education institutions in Czechia (CZ), Turkey (TR), and Slovakia (SK), allowing for a cross-national comparison of attitudes, perceived benefits and challenges, and ethical considerations. A mixed-methods design was applied, combining quantitative survey data with qualitative responses, analyzed using descriptive and thematic approaches. Results indicate that most students have used AI technologies, more frequently in CZ and SK than in TR. The most common use was to enhance general understanding of academic topics. Students identified accessibility as the main benefit of AI, while key concerns included AI bias in CZ and AI misuse in TR and SK. Most participants perceived limited ethical awareness among students and emphasized the need for institutional guidelines to promote responsible AI use. Students also viewed teachers as moderately or less willing to integrate AI into teaching and learning.

TI An ontological turn: being and becoming with digital technologies in
   education
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital technology; ontology; ontological turn; generative artificial
   intelligence; digital dilemma; expansive; teacher education; Digital
   technology; ontology; ontological turn; generative artificial
   intelligence; digital dilemma; expansive; teacher education
ID BLACK-BOX; COMPETENCE; KNOWLEDGE
AB In this conceptual paper, we explore how an ontological turn in the field of educational technology might contribute with an expansive perspective on digital technology. We base our argument on three perspectives on technology in education as we find them across existing research and frameworks: 1) Digital skills/competences perspective, 2) Pedagogical perspective, 3) Societal/humanistic perspective. In addition, we argue for an existing epistemological undercurrent running through research and frameworks. Through examples of a pressing influx of digital dilemmas, created particularly by generative artificial intelligence (AI), we continue to argue that AI's inescapable presence leaves us with a series of dilemmas that are either ontological in nature or carry ontological implications. Our ontological perspective differs from ontology or ontological engineering as understood in computer science as we build our understanding of ontology on psychology and anthropology. Our use of AI is driven by desires for efficiency, dialog and learning without us really knowing how AI produces its output. The fact that AI can "think" for us, mimic us and even replicate us, highlights an ontological question: what does it really mean to be human in a world where we do not have full control over the technology we created? This gives rise to our argument that teacher education must expand the perspective on technology by making an ontological turn in how technology is addressed.

TI The nature and dimensions of L2 identity in Iranian EFL context: a
   mixed-methods study using MLIQ
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Identity; language identity; multidimensional L2 identity questionnaire
   (MLIQ); second language identity dimensions (SLID); second language
   identity model (SLIM); Identity; language identity; multidimensional L2
   identity questionnaire (MLIQ); second language identity dimensions
   (SLID); second language identity model (SLIM)
ID LANGUAGE; TEACHERS
AB Due to the impact of different L2 identity dimensions on forming a unified language identity, thestudy followed an explanatory mixed-methods design to investigate levels of different L2 identity dimensions of Iranian EFL learners. A sample of 1,018 purposively selected learners filled out a researcher-made Questionnaire (MLIQ), and 30 of them took part in an Interview phase. PCA was used to determine the construct validity of the MLIQ, and the model fit of the data was determined through the SEM, using the AMOS. Data analysis using descriptive statistics and qualitative interpretations revealed that Iranian EFL learners had moderate levels of L2 identity with higher levels of homogeneous, overt, convergent, dynamic, intransitive, and inclusion SLID and an average level of active vs. passive dimension. The results of the interview questions showed that EFL learners developed their L2 identities more systematically and expanded their knowledge on social, national and cognitive dimensions to manifest their balanced L2 identity dimensions. Language learners and teachers can utilize the findings and balance their in-between and transitional identities in a way that they can protect their original and hybrid language identities and foster them through other complementary identities, in non-threatening manners, toward a more positive continuum on SLID.

TI Multimodal teachers behaviors in online music classes for Chinese
   primary and secondary schools: an analysis of six demonstration videos
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Music education; music classroom; instructional practices; multimodal;
   teacher behavior
ID CLASSROOM; EDUCATION; MANAGEMENT
AB While music classrooms are vital to aesthetic education in China, empirical investigation into the instructional practices within them remains limited. To illuminate current pedagogical characteristics, a multimodal analysis was conducted on six music demonstration lessons from the National Smart Education Platform for Primary and Secondary Schools (NSEPPSS). The analysis reveals two key patterns in teaching. First, although educators employed a variety of modalities, verbal instruction was the dominant method. Non-verbal modalities like eye contact, gestures, and PowerPoint slides served supplementary roles. In stark contrast, embodied practices such as demonstrative singing and rhythmic gestures-often considered vital to music pedagogy-were underutilized. Second, significant differences in modality use emerged across educational levels. The most pronounced divergence in teaching behaviors occurred between primary and middle school, whereas the patterns of middle and high school teachers were more closely aligned. Consequently, educators should place greater emphasis on the potential of non-verbal and embodied modalities, which can reinforce instruction and diversify expressive repertoires. Rather than over-relying on a single mode like spoken language, teachers should purposefully select modalities best suited to the learning objective. Fostering synergy between different modes is crucial, as their effective combination can stimulate student interest and cultivate a more engaging learning environment.

AB In response to evolving labor market demands, soft skills such as communication, teamwork, critical thinking and emotional intelligence have become as vital as technical expertise for higher education graduates. This study investigates how soft skills are understood, taught and assessed by faculty members in Kazakhstani universities, as well as the institutional, cultural and policy factors shaping their integration. TI Emotion regulation strategies among Saudi university students: exploring
   cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Cognitive reappraisal; cultural norms; emotion regulation; expressive
   suppression; gender differences; Saudi university students; Educational
   psychology; Higher education; Philosophy of education
ID INTELLIGENCE; STRESS
AB This study investigated the prevalence and patterns of cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression as emotion regulation strategies among Saudi university students. A cross-sectional research design was employed, with data collected from 330 participants using the 'Emotion Regulation Questionnaire' and demographic information. Descriptive statistics revealed moderate utilization of both strategies, with cognitive reappraisal (M = 3.08) being employed slightly more than expressive suppression (M = 2.94). Independent-sample t-tests and one-way ANOVA were conducted to examine differences in strategy use across gender, field of study (STEM vs. non-STEM), academic performance, and university level. Results indicated a statistically significant difference in cognitive reappraisal based on gender, with female students reporting higher engagement than male students (p = 0.008). However, no significant differences were found across other demographic variables for either strategy. These findings suggest that while Saudi university students moderately engage in both cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression, gender influences the use of cognitive reappraisal. The study confirms the need for culturally sensitive interventions promoting adaptive emotion regulation to improve students' well-being and academic success. Future research should explore additional strategies, demographic intersections, and longitudinal changes in emotion regulation within the Saudi university context.

TI Factors influencing the late submission of assignments in a medical
   university environment: a qualitative case study
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Procrastination; medical school assignments; undergraduate medical
   education; medical students; medical school
ID PREDICTING PERFORMANCE; DISCIPLINARY ACTION; RISK-FACTORS; STUDENTS;
   EDUCATION; SCHOOL; INTERVENTION; BEHAVIOR; PROGRAM; IMPACT
AB The late submission of assignments by medical students is a chronic problem. Students' characteristics and past academic performances are useful indicators for predicting delays during medical school. However, medical students' perspectives on factors that lead to delays in assignment submission remain unexplored. To address this issue, this study examines the factors that influence the late submission of assignments in a medical university setting from the perspective of medical students. This exploratory qualitative case study recruited 20 undergraduate medical students who had submitted their assignments late at a private Japanese medical university. Data were collected through face-to-face, semi-structured interviews and analyzed using thematic analysis from a constructivist paradigm. A qualitative analysis revealed the following three themes regarding the factors influencing the late submission of assignments: (1) factors related to the medical university curriculum, including its structure, course offerings, and academic requirements, (2) factors related to the instructions from and authority of faculty, and (3) situational factors that exacerbate delays in student assignment submissions. Medical students felt that the nature of the assignments, which were assigned with no apparent regard for student schedules and offered a limited evaluative metric, was often irrational. The students implicitly accepted this situation while being aware of the infeasible submission deadlines. Medical students may have an internal sense of the perceived irrationality of faculty-imposed assignments and the authority behind them, and may strategically neglect some in favor of efficient course completion. Faculty members should ensure their assignments are consistent with course contents.

TI The 'roots/routes to fruit' model: developing a 'fruitful' collaborative
   network across universities
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Significant networks; collective autoethnography; higher education;
   cross-national perspectives; collaborative networks
ID QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; CONVERSATIONS
AB This study explores the development and dynamics of the Wales Collaborative for Learning Design (WCLD), a multidisciplinary network across eight Welsh universities. Funded by Welsh Government, the WCLD aimed to foster collaboration in digital learning design while supporting individual and collective academic growth. The study aimed to investigate what factors impact on the development and sustainability of a personal and professional, multidisciplinary Higher Education collaborative network. Using a collective autoethnographic approach, the research explored the network's evolution, highlighting the interplay of person attributes, facilitating conditions, and professional relationships. Findings revealed key factors including trust, open-mindedness, and consistent communication as essential to the network's sustainability and success. Further findings illustrate how positive constraints, diverse career stages, and interdisciplinary opportunities underpin growth and productivity. 'Outcomes' included enhanced institutional impact, significant personal and professional conversations, and the cross-pollination of ideas within and beyond the network. When considered as a process, the findings underscore the value of cultivating intentional, yet adaptable, collaborative networks to support higher education innovation and personal academic development. This culminates in the 'Roots/routes to Fruit' model. This original contribution builds on existing theory surrounding significant, collaborative networks and provides a process for future interdisciplinary, multi-institutional, collaborative networks to build upon.

TI Exploring the barriers to implementing hybrid learning in rural primary
   schools
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Hybrid learning; rural education; educational challenges; constructivist
   pedagogy; ecological systems theory
ID CHALLENGES; MALAYSIA
AB Hybrid learning is a progressive approach that offers flexibility and expanded learning opportunities for students. However, limited attention has been given to the contextual barriers faced by rural primary schools in adopting such models. This study explores the barriers that hindered the implementation of hybrid learning during the Covid-19 pandemic in Malaysian rural primary schools. Employing a qualitative design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 19 rural primary school teachers to capture their experiences and perspectives on the challenges encountered by both students and teachers. Thematic analysis revealed four key themes, which are access and delivery challenges, assessment and engagement difficulties, increased teacher workload and stress, and parental involvement challenges. The study deepens understanding of the place-based obstacles affecting hybrid learning adoption within rural educational context and offers insights to strengthen systemic support structures and improve current education policies to promote digital equity and enhance the long-term viability of hybrid learning models for rural primary schools.

TI Assessing the correspondence of the basic science curriculum across the
   different classes with core curriculum specifications in Ebonyi State,
   Nigeria
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Correspondence; basic science curriculum; core curriculum;
   specifications; secondary schools
ID EDUCATION; INSTRUCTION
AB This study examines how the basic science curriculum in various classes in Ebonyi State, Nigeria, corresponds with the specification of the core curriculum. The study utilized a quantitative research approach and document analysis as part of a descriptive research design. A non-proportional stratified sample of 30 schools (15 public and 15 private) was selected from among the 583 secondary schools (343 private and 240 public). The data for the study were collected from the Ebonyi State Secondary Education Board's Basic Science curriculum and the Federal Ministry of Education's core curriculum. The degree of correspondence of the curriculum between JSS1, JSS2, and JSS3 was analyzed using descriptive statistics. The results show that the second term of JSS1 achieved a 100% level of correspondence, while the first and third terms revealed mixed levels, indicating a significant difference in curriculum correspondence. Also, there was a significant difference between JSS2's three terms, and in JSS3, there is a high level of correspondence between the taught syllabus and the core curriculum. Based on the findings, it is therefore recommended that educational stakeholders look into the correspondence of the curriculum to improve its effectiveness in secondary schools in Nigeria for a better learning outcome.

TI Assessing the role of entrepreneurship education in fostering innovation
   and new venture creation: the moderating role of financial literacy
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Entrepreneurship education; financial literacy; innovation; new venture
   creation; Oman Vision 2040; Entrepreneurship education; financial
   literacy; innovation; new venture creation; Oman Vision 2040
ID INTENTIONS; ATTITUDES; VARIABLES; BUSINESS; IMPACT
AB This study investigates how entrepreneurship education (EE) influences innovation (IN) and new venture creation (NVC), with financial literacy (FL) examined as a potential moderating factor among university students in Oman. The research responds to the pressing need for effective educational interventions to enhance entrepreneurial outcomes among youth, particularly within the context of economic diversification strategies like Oman Vision 2040. Adopting a quantitative approach, data were collected from 213 students enrolled in entrepreneurship-related programs, and structural equation modelling was used to analyse relationships among the variables. The results reveal that EE has a significant positive effect on both IN (beta = 0.531, p < 0.001) and NVC (beta = 0.478, p < 0.001), highlighting the importance of structured entrepreneurial learning in driving innovation and venture creation. However, FL did not significantly moderate the relationships between EE and either IN or NVC. This suggests that financial literacy, in isolation, may not substantially enhance entrepreneurial outcomes unless embedded within experiential or contextual learning. The study concludes that while entrepreneurship education is a critical driver of innovation and new ventures, its effectiveness can be enhanced by integrating practical, real-world financial applications. It recommends that policymakers and educators focus on experiential learning models and cross-disciplinary curricula to better equip students for entrepreneurial success.

TI Academic research careers for medical doctors (ARC-MD): a five-year UC
   Davis training program to foster the next generation of
   physician-scientists
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Longitudinal curriculum; mentorship; research skills; workforce
   development; physician-scientist
AB Since the establishment of the Flexnerian model of medical education, single degree (MD) physician-scientists have significantly advanced biomedical research and clinical medicine. However, institutional emphasis has predominantly favoured dual-degree MD/PhD Medical Scientist Training Programs (MSTPs). Recognizing that many successful academic physician-scientists do not hold PhDs, there remains a critical need for structured research training and mentorship targeting single degree students. The University of California Davis School of Medicine developed the Academic Research Careers for Medical Doctors (ARC-MD) program as part of a broader institutional strategy to accelerate innovation, aligning closely with an institutional framework emphasizing thematic breadth and reciprocal interactions between basic and clinical departments. ARC-MD strategically integrates a five-year research-intensive pathway into the traditional four-year MD curriculum, annually enrolling 4-8 students. The program includes an introductory pre-matriculation course, a longitudinal curriculum spanning medical school, focused mentorship fostering interdisciplinary collaboration, a dedicated research year emphasizing reciprocal exchanges between clinical and basic science research, professional identity formation, and financial support through tuition scholarships and stipends. Since its inception in 2019, ARC-MD has enrolled 41 students and graduated two cohorts. Program evaluation surveys were administered in 2024 and 2025 across all five years of training. Student-reported research self-efficacy, measured using the Clinical Research Appraisal Inventory, was lowest among newly matriculating students (pre-program) and increased in subsequent years. Student-reported identity as physician-scientists and student assessments of mentors also showed overall improvement across training levels, though trajectories were not strictly linear.

TI Intrinsic versus extrinsic motivation in EFL: a mixed-methods approach
   to the university students in the Uzbek context
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE EFL learning; intrinsic motivation; extrinsic motivation; mixed-methods
   research; Uzbekistan
ID GENDER-DIFFERENCES; 2ND-LANGUAGE; LEARNERS; ENGLISH; FOREIGN
AB Motivation is a key determinant of success in foreign language learning, yet its dynamics in Central Asian contexts remain underexplored. This study investigates the balance between intrinsic and extrinsic motivational factors among English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners at Fergana State University, Uzbekistan. A mixed-methods design was employed, combining data from 301 fourth-year English majors using a validated questionnaire and semi-structured interviews. Quantitative findings revealed that intrinsic motivation (M = 4.12, SD = 0.68) was significantly stronger than extrinsic motivation (M = 3.74, SD = 0.81), t(300) = 6.82, p < .001. Cognitive stimulation emerged as the most powerful motivator (85.8% agreement), while parental expectations had the weakest effect (28.5%). Qualitative analysis identified four key themes: cognitive engagement, personal growth, practical benefits, and cultural exploration. A modest yet significant correlation was found between intrinsic motivation and self-reported proficiency (r = 0.28, p < .001), whereas extrinsic motivation showed no significant link. Gender analysis revealed no notable differences despite the female-majority sample (83%). Overall, the findings highlight that EFL pedagogy in Uzbekistan should foster intellectual curiosity and personal development while acknowledging learners' career aspirations, contributing to a clearer understanding of motivational dynamics in Central Asian higher education.

DE Computer skills; prisoners; incarceration; rehabilitation; inclusive and
   equitable economy
ID REHABILITATION
AB People proved guilty of crimes are punished and reformed by prison sentences. Convicts are assigned mostly manual labour, for which they receive pitiful compensation. Additionally, they receive vocational training to aid them carry out delegated activities. Once released, they are unprepared for civil society's animosity and rejection. Most of them get dragged back into the web of crime. Corporations need individuals who can profitably contribute to and help them keep up with fierce competition. It becomes extremely challenging for the inmate to get acceptance and employment, and raises concerns on the sustainability aspects in Civic Society post release. Hence the current study aimed to make the inmates ready to combat these challenges. Computer Training was imparted for their social reintegration in the Prisons in Maharashtra. This report examined the different training and rehabilitation programs implemented in Maharashtra's jail system. In the methodology, Purposive sampling method was used since it involves the detailed investigation of prisoner's rehabilitation and vocational training in India. There were three batches of inmates who had undergone the training across all the prisons. Batch sizes varied as per the requirements for the training and were therefore 8, 10, and 14 respectively. For the study, samples were drawn from the inmates who were closer to their release from the Prison. Thus, purposive sampling was used for imparting computer-based trainings. Data was collected through a mixed methods approach. The findings showed that the computer-based trainings were viewed very positively both by the prisoners as also in the focused group discussion and were regarded as necessary for better reintegration into civil society post release. Researchers advocate vocational training and rehabilitation strategies based on their detailed examination of prison programs, company readiness to hire ex-convicts, comments from NGOs, and prisoners themselves. These measures will lead to a more inclusive, egalitarian, and sustainable society.

TI "PEI-ICF PETRA": a smart web platform to foster cooperation in drafting
   the individualized Education Plan (IEP) for students with disability
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Educational digital tool; students with disabilities (DWDs);
   individualized educational plan (IEP); international classification of
   functioning; disability and health (ICF); Social Sciences; Education;
   Behavioral Sciences; Educational Psychology; Cognitive Psychology;
   Motivation
ID CHILDREN; CY; PARTICIPATION; PROGRAMS; SCHOOL
AB The implementation of the framework offered by the international classification of functioning disability and health (ICF) is recognized as a necessary step in the process of school inclusion for pupils with disabilities. This step may be greatly eased by informatics tools that guide users without requiring extensive familiarity with the ICF. Here we describe the development and testing of PETRA, a specific digital tool that supports the personalization of the educational path for students with certified disabilities in Italy. The tool foresees the active participation of the family and the student himself in his own training path and guides the user through sequential steps: observation, planning, realization, validation, The usability and efficiency of the tool was tested in a representative set of schools in the Trento province. Using this tool, each student is considered in his uniqueness and the educational and didactic interventions are calibrated to its specificities (including the oftenunrecognized potentialities,) and the context in which it lives. The tool was well received, showed its efficiency in each of the steps promising to offer substantial support in improving school inclusion and empowerment of students with disabilities.

TI Assessing help-seeking strategies among nontraditional learners in
   distance education
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Nontraditional learners; help-seeking strategies; self-regulated
   learning; online education; academic support; demographic factors
AB Online education has significantly expanded in the United States, with enrollment in online programs among college students rising from 26% in 2013 to 73% in 2020. Nontraditional learners, including part-time students, full-time employees and first-generation students, face higher attrition and lower graduation rates. Self-regulated learning, particularly help-seeking strategies, is crucial to academic success. Using a quantitative, correlational design, this study examined the relationship between help-seeking strategies, GPA, demographics and class standing among online first-year nontraditional learners at A.T. Still University in the United States. A total of 33 out of the 231 first-year students enrolled participated in the study. Data from a stratified random sample were analyzed using Spearman's Rank-order Correlation, the Chi-square Test of Independence and the Kruskal-Wallis H Test. Results showed a weak positive correlation between GPA and formal help-seeking strategies. In contrast, informal strategies had minimal use and a weak negative correlation. Demographic factors influenced preferences, with structured resources favored by married and employed students. Institutions should prioritize accessible digital resources and faculty engagement to support success.

TI Adaption and Validation of the Behaviors, Related Attitudes, and
   Intentions Toward Science-survey (BRAINS) for Albanian-speaking students
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Attitudes; science; survey; validity; student beliefs; Testing,
   Measurement and Assessment; Science Education; Secondary Education
ID SECONDARY-SCHOOL STUDENTS; CHILDRENS ATTITUDES; GENDER-DIFFERENCES;
   HONG-KONG; GRADES 5; CHEMISTRY; ACHIEVEMENT; TEACHERS; BIOLOGY
AB A primary focus of scientific education studies has been investigating students' attitudes toward pursuing scientific knowledge, which drives a strong interest in fostering positive attitudes toward science and promoting scientific education. This study provides a comprehensive description of the process of adapting and validating the Behaviors, Related Attitudes, and Intentions toward Science (BRAINS) survey to assess the attitudes toward science of pre-college Albanian-speaking students of natural sciences in Kosovo's lower-education system. The original version of BRAINS, developed by Summers and Abd-El-Khalick (2018) has been proven reliable by the criteria of current psychometric evaluation and theoretical background. This study employed CFA to assess construct validity of the original survey. The BRAINS survey may be customized for the Kosovar context to emphasize the pertinent beliefs, actions, and intentions of students regarding science and how these impact their performance and decision-making.

TI A comparative study of community service integration in high school
   education: insights from Malaysian and Indonesian teachers' practices
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Administration; community service; high school; Indonesia; Malaysia
ID PROGRAM
AB This study presents a comparative analysis of community service integration in schools across Indonesia and Malaysia, examining distinct methods, challenges, and outcomes in different educational settings. Through semi-structured interviews with 13 participants-seven from Indonesia (teachers, a school principal, a program coordinator, and students) and six from Malaysia (teachers, a program coordinator, and students)-we explored how cultural values, national policies, and institutional goals shape community service implementation. Thematic analysis revealed significant differences: Indonesian schools employ highly structured, curriculum-integrated programs, particularly in vocational education where initiatives emphasize long-term skill development. Malaysian schools adopt a flexible, collaborative approach, partnering with external organizations to provide diverse community engagement opportunities that emphasize social interaction and civic responsibility. Findings indicate that Indonesia's structured model excels at fostering practical competencies and readiness for future careers, while Malaysia's collaborative model cultivates broader community awareness and social responsibility. Common challenges include resource limitations, insufficient teacher training, and difficulties assessing long-term impact. This research suggests that a hybrid approach combining structured skill-building with flexible collaboration could enhance the effectiveness of community service in both countries and comparable educational contexts.

TI Teaching and learning in new spaces: the pedagogy-suited learning space
   approach
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE New pedagogy; teaching methods; learning spaces; learning outside the
   classroom; modern classrooms; PSLS
AB Technological developments alongside global crises have affected education systems worldwide, including Israel, with a growing need to develop teaching methods and tools adapted to the current generation. Traditional teaching, which was primarily the transfer of knowledge through rote learning, evolved into teaching that is primarily creativity and entrepreneurship based on methods to develop skills of reasoning, discourse and self-expression, and creativity, responsibility and engagement. Concurrently, technological and industrial developments, together with aging buildings, have led to the renovation and new construction of classrooms and learning spaces. Despite the numerous innovations in teaching, teachers seem to be using traditional teaching methods even in these new spaces, or are using new methods in traditional classrooms, retaining the teacher-centric approaches of the past. This situation highlights the need to examine teachers' teaching methods, role perceptions, practice, teacher training to use the new methods and whether their teaching methods are suitable for the physical spaces in which they teach. The current study examines physical spaces and the teaching that takes place in them. Its goal is to describe learning spaces that are not traditional classrooms and reviews the teaching methods in these spaces, in order to spark contemplation about teaching effectiveness in new learning spaces, and to shed light on the need to adapt pedagogical methods to the physical space in which these methods are applied, and to adjust existing learning spaces to pedagogical, social and emotional goals, in order to shape the future design of learning spaces. Such adjustments must also match school needs and align with the training programs that prepare teachers for working in such spaces. The study, employing a field-based qualitative approach, describes six types of indoor and outdoor physical learning spaces and includes observations in 12 lessons in grades 3-6 in elementary schools in Israel in the south, north and center of Israel. The learning spaces were documented visually and teaching methods and pupils' activities were recorded in writing. The findings of the study potentially have practical implications for the work of teachers, principals, policymakers and the work of architects and designers involved in the design of learning spaces. The insights arising from this study potentially contribute to the design process of new learning spaces or reorganization of existing learning spaces to ensure that the needs of the school, the teachers and the pupils are accurately addressed in a manner that serves pedagogy and supports a pupil-centric approach in each lesson, and help teachers improve their teaching practice and customize it to pupils' needs. The study also stresses the need to rethink teachers' professional training programs, and their training in pedagogy-suited teaching. The findings presented in this article contributed to the development of the pedagogy-suited learning spaces model. While the full model was developed based on a broader mixed-methods study, this article focuses solely on the qualitative findings-observations and interviews-that supported the model's conceptualization.

TI Exploring the perceptions and alternative models in accessing primary
   education for Datooga pastoralists in Karatu District, Tanzania
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Alternative models; perceptions; access; pastoral Datooga; primary
   education
AB This study used the Human Rights Theory as a framework to examine the perceptions and alternative education models among the Datooga, a small pastoral community in northern and central Tanzania. A qualitative case study design was adopted, involving 48 participants, including educational officers, government officials, school heads, parents, and pupils, selected through purposive sampling. Data collection methods included semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, and document reviews, with thematic analysis applied to the data. Findings revealed that the Datooga pastoralists prioritise livestock herding over education, reflecting negative attitudes toward formal schooling. To improve access to primary education, the study identified three alternative models: establishing boarding schools, providing school meals, and introducing alternative basic education programs. Boarding schools, in particular, were emphasised as essential to reduce the burden of long commutes for children. The study also highlighted the need for a national policy tailored to pastoralists to ensure greater educational access. Additionally, education stakeholders are urged to raise awareness within the Datooga and similar communities about the value of primary education. The study underscores the importance of culturally sensitive approaches and government support in addressing educational challenges faced by pastoralist groups.

TI Effects of a 16-week structured functional music-based physical activity
   program on attitude toward sports among rural Chinese high school
   students: a quasi-experimental study
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Functional music; exercise attitudes; rural adolescents; physical
   activity; quasi-experimental study; Social Sciences; Area Studies;
   Education; Curriculum Studies; Physical Education
ID EXERCISE
AB This study examined the impact of a 16-week Structured Functional Music-Based Physical Activity (FMPA) program on attitudes toward sports among rural Chinese high school students. Using a quasi-experimental design, a total of 98 first-year students from a rural high school in Henan Province were assigned to either an intervention group (n = 50) or a control group (n = 48). The intervention group participated in FMPA sessions five times weekly, while the control group engaged in routine collective running. Attitudes were measured using the revised exercise attitude scale (EAS), assessing affective experience, behavioral intention, and behavioral cognition, with assessments conducted before and after the program. ANCOVA results, adjusted for baseline scores, indicated that the FMPA group showed greater improvements in behavioral intention (p = 0.032, d = 0.51) and total attitude (p = 0.008, d = 0.58). The findings suggest that functional music-integrated physical activity had a significant positive effect on attitudes toward sports in rural adolescent populations.

   education; Social Sciences; Education; Higher Education; Study of Higher
   Education; Teaching & Learning

AB This paper addresses the critical gap in preparing university educators to integrate entrepreneurship across various disciplines. Despite policy pushes for widespread entrepreneurship education, a significant barrier is the lack of adequately prepared faculty who feel confident in adapting and delivering entrepreneurial elements within their specific disciplines. This paper presents a teacher professional development program and explores its immediate and long-term impact on participating educators. The training is grounded in constructivist active and experiential learning approaches and aims to empower university educators across disciplines to incorporate entrepreneurial elements into their educational practices. The study uses a mixed-methods approach, combining pre- and post-training surveys with follow-up focus-group interviews conducted several months after course completion. The evaluation is based on the Kirkpatrick model, assessing participants' reactions, learning, behaviour, and results. Quantitative findings indicate initial positive effects on reaction and learning among participants. Qualitative analyses from focus-group interviews reveal sustained learning and changes in teaching behaviours, which have led to positive impacts on student outcomes across diverse fields. These findings support the value of training university educators to foster embedded entrepreneurship education in higher education.

TI Psychological capital as a catalyst: Unlocking job satisfaction,
   embeddedness, and performance among international faculty
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Faculty job satisfaction; international faculty; psychological capital;
   job embeddedness; faculty performance; well-being
ID IMPACT; PEOPLE
AB The motivation of teaching faculty is essential for the effective functioning of the education system, especially in multicultural environments. To stay motivated, faculty need strong psychological capital (PsyCap) and a sense of professional fulfillment. However, integrating multinational teams can be challenging due to cultural biases and misinterpretations. There is a notable research gap in understanding how PsyCap varies across cultures and influences motivation in diverse educational settings. This study aims to develop the theory of PsyCap, explore its integration into the education workforce, and examine its application in multicultural teaching contexts. Data were collected from 300 faculty members from different parts of the United Arab Emirates. A structural equation modeling approach was used to test the proposed relationships. The results showed a strong relationship between psychological capital, job embeddedness, job satisfaction, and job performance among international faculty. The findings may enhance psychological capital across organizations. The practical implication of this findings support linking psychological capital to performance evaluations. Rather than focusing solely on traditional KPIs like research output and teaching scores, supervisors can discuss psychological strengths and growth areas. This approach aligns personal goals with institutional missions, enhancing performance, well-being, and leadership, and yielding both material and spiritual rewards.

AB Understanding atomic structures is a fundamental aspect of chemistry education, yet students often struggle to understand these concepts abstract concepts due to limited access to hands-on instructional tools. Specifically, it explores teachers' and students' perceptions andevaluate teachers' pedagogical practices. . TI Pedagogical quality of geography lesson delivery in Rwandan secondary
   schools
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Geography; lesson delivery; secondary education; school types; Rwanda
AB The study explored the quality of secondary school geography lesson delivery, lesson structure, teaching methods, teaching aids, classroom management and assessment practices to identify the best practices and areas for improvement across different school types- rural, urban, private, public, boarding and day schools. The study adopted a descriptive quantitative observational design. A purposive sampling technique was used to select 20 secondary schools, four from each of Rwanda's four provinces and the City of Kigali, based on their distinct physical and human geographic characteristics. The sample included one private school, one public boarding school, and two public day schools in each region, ensuring balanced representation across different school types. One geography teacher of advanced level was purposively selected from each school, resulting in a total sample of 20 teachers observed. Data were analyzed using SPSS with descriptive statistics. Findings revealed notable disparities in relation to school types. Urban, private, and boarding schools generally outperformed rural and public day schools in lesson structure, teaching methods, use of teaching aids and classroom management. However, areas such as lesson introductions, classroom rules communication, integration of technology, lesson pacing, and assessment practices emerged as common challenges, particularly in rural and day schools. While teachers demonstrated strong alignment of teaching methods and assessments with lesson objectives, the use of diverse strategies, timely feedback, and effective technology integration remains limited. The findings underscore the need for targeted improvements to support competency-based geography education and ensure equitable learning outcomes across diverse school contexts.

TI Motivation or hygiene factors? Teachers' beliefs on salary as a
   motivator in Tanzania's secondary schools
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Beliefs; hygiene and motivator factors; public secondary teachers;
   salary; Tanzania; Beliefs; hygiene and motivator factors; public
   secondary teachers; salary; Tanzania
AB The influence of remuneration on teachers' motivation has drawn global attention. However, motivational theories such as Herzberg's two-factor theory have traditionally categorized money as a hygiene factor rather than a direct motivator. Nevertheless, the extent to which this classification holds true across different contexts remains a subject of inquiry. This study investigates secondary school teachers' beliefs in Arumeru District, Tanzania, about salary as a motivator or hygiene factor. Employing a phenomenological research design and qualitative approach, the study engaged a sample of 56 participants, comprising 49 teachers and 7 school heads. School heads were selected through purposive sampling, while teachers were chosen through convenience sampling. Data were collected via semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions, subsequently analyzed using thematic analysis. The results show that, contrary to Herzberg's theory, teachers view salary as a motivator that meets their needs and enhances job satisfaction. Teachers regard hygiene factors as external motivators contingent upon employers and coworkers. These findings challenge the application of Herzberg's theory in the Tanzanian context and suggest further research.

TI Students' academic struggles in solving trigonometry problems: an
   investigative study on students' programs of study
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic performance; program of study; trigonometry word problems;
   mixed-method analysis; Ghanaian SHS
ID EXPECTANCY-VALUE THEORY; MOTIVATION
AB Trigonometry remains one of the most challenging topics in the Ghanaian mathematics curriculum, with many students facing challenges in their quest to comprehend and solve related problems. Notable differences in student performance across academic programs prompted this study, which explored how students' program of study in senior high school influences their academic performance in trigonometry problem-solving and examined the factors behind program-based variations in students' trigonometry performance. Utilising a mixed-method approach, a sample of 100 final-year high school students underwent assessment via a Trigonometry Achievement Test (TAT). Descriptive and inferential statistical analyses were employed for the quantitative data, while qualitative responses were analysed thematically. ANOVA results showed statistically significant differences in performance by academic program (alpha = 0.05, F (5,94) = 56.04, p < 0.01), with General Science students performing the highest and Home Economics students performing the lowest. The qualitative analysis revealed several factors contributing to these differences, including students' perceived relevance of trigonometry to their future careers, levels of motivation and interest, peer influence, and study habits. These findings suggest that students' academic programs shape both their engagement with mathematics and their success in solving trigonometric problems.

TI Blame attribution and accountability in Palestinian academic discourse:
   a discursive analysis of student-instructor communication
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Student-teacher communication; academic evaluations; blame attribution;
   accountability; discursive analysis; academic performance; Social
   Psychology; Applied Linguistics; Interdisciplinary Language Studies
ID FAILURE
AB This research examines how Palestinian university students use discursive practices to negotiate blame and accountability with their instructors regarding academic performance. Drawing on discursive psychology, the study analyzed student messages to explore how they explain low grades and negotiate outcomes. Three primary discourses were identified: Expectation Discrepancy, Should-Be-Otherwise, and Failure-as-Something-Else. Findings show that students frequently shift responsibility for poor performance onto external factors, such as instructors' decisions, socio-economic pressures, and societal expectations. They employ discursive devices, including contrasts, extreme case formulations, and stake inoculation, to manage their academic identities and mitigate personal accountability. The study highlights the socio-cultural and economic contexts shaping students' perspectives in Palestine, where academic success is often viewed not solely as an individual effort but as linked to familial, societal, and economic pressures. By examining these discourses, the research contributes to understanding how culture and socio-economic conditions intersect with education, shaping accountability and identity management. The findings underscore the importance of considering these broader contextual factors in studies of student discourse and call for future research to investigate how similar practices manifest across diverse educational settings globally.

TI The complex interplay between international collaboration and scientific
   impact: evidence from the Scopus database
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Scientific impact; international collaboration; quantile regression;
   Scopus database
ID CITATION IMPACT; CO-AUTHORSHIP; LARGE-SCALE; SCIENCE; PATTERNS;
   PUBLICATION; INDICATOR; NETWORK; GROWTH; WEB
AB The widely held assumption that international collaboration boosts scientific impact oversimplifies a more complex relationship. This study examines how different levels of international collaboration affect the citation impact of the most productive countries and research fields, based on Scopus data from 1996 to 2017. Both field-normalized and non-normalized citation metrics are employed. While international collaboration and scientific impact are highly correlated under standard linear regression, such models fail to capture the skewed and heteroskedastic nature of citation distributions. To address this limitation, we apply pooled quantile regression with panel data covering 23 countries. Three key findings emerge: (i) Higher levels of international collaboration are generally associated with increased citation impact across quantiles. However, this effect varies substantially across disciplines, even among highly productive fields such as Medicine, Physics, Engineering, and Computer Science, suggesting that field-specific citation practices, rather than collaboration per se, may drive the observed differences; (ii) When using field-normalized metrics, the increasing effect of collaboration across quantiles largely disappears; (iii) Significant regional disparities emerge when controlling for geography through dummy variables. These findings challenge the validity of one-size-fits-all collaboration policies and underscore the importance of tailoring science strategies to each country's research capacity and disciplinary strengths. The study offers actionable insights for evidence-based science and innovation policymaking.

TI Evaluating the empowerment of PhD students in online courses on
   responsible conduct of research: an exploratory study
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Responsible conduct of research; empowerment; training; Small Private
   Online Course (SPOC); PhD training; research integrity; Assessment;
   Philosophy of Education; Research Methods in Education
ID RESEARCH ETHICS EDUCATION; PERSPECTIVES; INTEGRITY; FUTURE
AB This exploratory study explores if online courses can empower PhD students in Responsible Conduct of Research (RCR). We evaluated three Small Private Online Courses (SPOCs) with a specific focus on active collaboration of participants and critical reflection. The evaluation targeted key RCR competencies: awareness, knowledge, reflection, motivation, courage and the ability to handle integrity issues in research practice. Using a mixed-method approach, we gathered data from PhD student participants through surveys (n = 120), learner reports (n = 72), semi-structured interviews (n = 7) and case reflections (n = 40). Findings indicate that participants across all three courses reported increased competence in multiple aspects of RCR. The results suggest that thoughtfully designed online courses can meaningfully support RCR empowerment among early-career researchers. IMPACT STATEMENT In this study, we inquire in three online thematic courses that were developed for PhD candidates if the teaching philosophy to empower the candidates towards responsible conduct of research is successful. We found support, comparable to another study on another online course, for the thought that participants can be empowered and become critically autonomous in research integrity dilemmas, and that we can help build researchers' capacities and empower them to consistently adopt responsible, transparent and accountable behavior as the standard for their research endeavors.

TI Teaching critical thinking skills in Rwandan secondary schools:
   challenge and practical solutions
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Critical thinking skills; teaching critical thinking; critical thinking
   assessment; Kiswahili; 21st century skills; Social Sciences; Language
   Education; Classroom Practice; Assessment and Testing; Teaching and
   Learning
AB Many university graduates struggle with critical thinking due to weak secondary school preparation, affecting their independent reasoning and decision-making. This study examined the level of critical thinking skills among Kiswahili secondary school students, factors affecting their development, and challenges in teaching these skills. A mixed-methods design was employed, combining quantitative data from a literature-based test taken by 91 senior six students with qualitative data from document analysis, classroom observations, and interviews with five Kiswahili teachers. The test assessed both foundational skills (remembering, understanding, and applying) and higher-order thinking skills (analyzing, evaluating, and creating) based on Revised Bloom's Taxonomy. Results indicated low proficiency in higher-order skills (as low as 17%) compared to foundational skills (up to 67.1%). This gap was linked to poor instructional practices, including inadequate lesson planning, rote-based assessments, insufficient teacher training, and limited Kiswahili literary materials. The study recommends strengthening teacher training to support learner-centered lesson plans and better use of available ressources to enhance students' analytical, evaluative, and creative abilities. As the study was conducted to one district, findings may be generalized. Further research in other districts is recommended to validate these findings.

TI A structural equation model of English learning: exploring the
   relationship of second language motivation, foreign language enjoyment
   and learning engagement among Chinese college students
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE L2 motivation; foreign language enjoyment; learning engagement; Chinese
   college students; English learning; structural equation model; Social
   Sciences; Educational Psychology; Language Education; Motivation; Second
   Language Acquisition
ID ANXIETY; COLLINEARITY
AB As self-determination theory postulated, motivation has a close relationship with human behaviour. However, in second language (L2) acquisition context, the pattern of L2 motivation influencing students' behaviour in learning and the role of foreign language enjoyment (FLE) in this relationship are still unclear. Therefore, taking FLE as mediator, this study aims to explore the mechanism of L2 motivation impacting learning engagement among Chinese college students. Participants were 300 college students from China. A structural equation model was constructed using AMOS 28.0. Results showed that both L2 motivation and FLE are significant predictor of students' learning engagement, and FLE partially mediates the relationship between L2 motivation and learning engagement. The findings of this study emphasize the important role of L2 motivation and enjoyment in Chinse college students English learning. Theoretical and practical implications for educators and English teachers were discussed.

TI Exploring the learning effect on serial concept mapping with expert map
   sharing approach
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Concept map; serial concept map; re-composition; expert map sharing;
   knowledge representation; learning outcomes; Technology; Computer
   Science; Artificial Intelligence; Human-Computer Intelligence; Legal,
   Ethical & Social Aspects of IT; Human-Computer Interaction
ID TOOLS
AB This study explores the effectiveness of two concept mapping methods - re-composition and scratch-building - within a serial concept mapping framework enhanced by expert map sharing. Serial concept mapping integrates maps from consecutive classes into a cumulative structure, facilitating incremental knowledge development. Expert map sharing involves providing teacher-created maps representing a well-structured understanding of lecture content, shared after students create their own maps to reinforce comprehension. A comparative experiment was conducted over three weeks in six human-computer interaction (HCI) classes, involving 158 participants: three classes using the re-composition method (n=56) and three using the scratch-building method (n=102). The re-composition method provided predefined concepts and links extracted from the expert map, supporting alignment with learning objectives and reducing cognitive load. In contrast, the scratch-building method allowed for free map creation, fostering creativity but risking conceptual misalignment. While both groups showed comparable progress during weekly activities, result suggest that the re-composition method may enable better knowledge organization, as evidenced by statistically significant improvements in both overall scores (p=0.03) and higher-order thinking (HOT) performance (p=0.001) on summative tests, particularly for map-based content. These findings highlight the potential of re-composition method, combined with expert map sharing, as a promising approach for enhancing learning outcomes in serial concept mapping.

AB Students' difficulty in algebraic expressions is perhaps one of the underlying factors of their low performance in mathematics. TI A digitised framework for research-finance management in higher
   education institutions: insights from an autoethnographic study in South
   Africa
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Experiences; finance management; researchers' attitudes; institutional
   practices; universities; Social Sciences; Education; Higher Education;
   Study of Higher Education; Teaching & Learning
AB University research is increasingly dependent on effective finance management, yet much of the existing literature approaches this issue from institutional or administrative perspectives, with limited attention to the lived experiences of those directly engaged in research-finance processes. This gap restricts understanding of how policies and practices shape everyday research work. To address this, this study employs a collaborative autoethnographic approach drawing on the experiences of a research-finance professional, a research manager, and a researcher at a South African university. Reflections and real-time notes were analysed to identify key themes, including institutional policies, budgeting and disbursement, researcher attitudes, and accountability mechanisms. Findings show that effective communication, transparent disbursement, and digital monitoring tools are central to sustaining research quality and innovation, but challenges persist around compliance, resource allocation, and coordination between finance units and researchers. From these insights, the study proposes a digitised framework for research-finance management, complemented by practical action steps. This contribution highlights insider perspectives often absent from prior work and provide a context-specific yet adaptable model for strengthening research-finance systems in higher education.

ID CLASSROOM
AB Silence is a common occurrence in language learning that can cause frustration for teachers. The issue of silence has been extensively studied in traditional classroom settings, but it has become increasingly prevalent in online learning environments as technology has advanced. Several studies have been conducted on learners' perceptions and experiences of silence.    academic performance: neurological mechanisms and implementation
   strategies

ID MINDFULNESS; EXPERIENCE
AB Vipassana, an ancient mindfulness practice with its origin in Buddhism, has come out as a valuable approach for enhancing attention and emotional well-being. The applications of Vipassana in academia, particularly in enhancing attention and improving academic performances in students, have been explored in this paper.
