TI Shaping equity in the classroom: Investigating gender sensitivity in
   classroom interaction in Tanzanian secondary schools
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Gender responsive; pedagogy; classroom interaction; gender equity; and
   student participation in learning
AB This study investigated teachers' gender responsiveness in classroom interaction dynamics as a means to promote equitable student participation in the learning process. The research utilised a case study design within a qualitative research framework. A purposive stratified sampling method was employed to select 27 secondary school teachers. Data were collected through classroom observations and interviews and analysed through thematic data analysis techniques to generate themes that address the research questions. The results indicated varying levels of gender sensitivity in interaction patterns among secondary school teachers. The varying gender sensitivity was influenced by factors such as knowledge level and personal background. Additionally, cultural factors and teachers' attitudes towards one sex were observed to be major barriers to effective gender-conscious classroom interaction, as some teachers intentionally favour one gender. The study suggests incorporating gender-responsive content in pre- and in-service teacher education programmes to help teachers create an inclusive learning environment for all students.

TI The behavioral intentions to integrate AI in teaching science among
   distance and contact education student teachers: a comparative study
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; behavioral intentions; comparative descriptive
   survey; science student teachers; Artificial intelligence; behavioral
   intentions; comparative descriptive survey; science student teachers
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; TECHNOLOGY
AB Integrating Artificial Intelligence could reduce educational challenges and improve learning outcomes in teaching science. However, the intention of teachers to use these technologies is poorly understood. Informed by the Theory of Planned Behavior, this comparative survey study examined the behavioral intentions of science student teachers from two South African universities to integrate AI into teaching science. An online questionnaire was used to collect data from purposively sampled final-year students from Central University (n = 97) and East Coast University (n = 85). Data analysis involved Exploratory Factor Analysis to identify the structure of constructs, ordinal logistic regression to identify predictors of behavioral intention, and the Mann-Whitney U test to compare behavioral intentions between the two samples. The results suggested that the constructs conformed to the Theory of Planned Behavior with high reliability (Cronbach's Alpha: .846-.935). Seven factors explained 72.67% of the variance, with strong loadings. Both samples demonstrated a positive intention to integrate AI, with the Central University reporting higher control beliefs (p = .005). However, Ordinal Logistic Regression indicated the constructs did not significantly predict behavioral intentions (p > .05). The findings highlight the importance of providing context-specific training programs to support the integration of AI in science education. IMPACT STATEMENT This study examined South African science student teachers' intentions to integrate Artificial Intelligence (AI) into teaching, comparing distance and contact education contexts. The findings show strong readiness to embrace AI, highlighting opportunities for innovation in science education. However, differences in control beliefs reveal structural inequities in training, access, and support that shape confidence in AI adoption. By exposing these disparities, the study demonstrates the need for responsive, hands-on professional development and equitable resource provision. It advances educational practice and policy by offering evidence to strengthen AI integration, bridge systemic gaps, and promote sustainable, equitable improvements in science education.

TI Becoming data in education: the enactment of the homo oeconomicus
   through measuring
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Becoming data; intra-action; ideality; social measurements; homo
   oeconomicus
AB This article examines how educational measurement instruments in Chile-specifically the School Vulnerability Index (SVI), The complementary questionnaires of the System for Measuring the Quality of Education in Chile (SIMCE), and the complementary questionnaires of the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA)-function as algorithmic and material-discursive apparatuses that co-produce the categories they claim to assess. Drawing on posthumanist and feminist new materialist theories-particularly the works of Karen Barad and Sylvia Wynter-we argue that these measurements are not neutral but are embedded in state rationalities and global governance. Through a diffractive analysis of technical documents and interviews with measurement producers, we show how these instruments normalize subjectivities aligned with the neoliberal figure of homo oeconomicus, reframing inequality as individual risk. Categories like 'vulnerability' and 'ideal student' are not passively observed but actively constructed through socio-technical assemblages that displace structural critique in favor of predictive logic. By transforming students into datafied subjects and projecting their value as future capital, these instruments entrench social hierarchies while maintaining a discourse of objectivity. We call for rethinking educational measurement practices through epistemic justice, rejecting econometric rationalities in favor of relational, situated understandings of educational injustice.

TI Exploring the factors driving L1 use in Jordanian secondary EFL
   classrooms
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE L1 use; L2 classroom; EFL context; EFL teaching and learning; Jordanian
   education system; L1 use; L2 classroom; EFL context; EFL teaching and
   learning; Jordanian education system
ID FOREIGN-LANGUAGE; ENGLISH PROFICIENCY; ORAL PROFICIENCY; TEACHERS;
   SCHOOL; LEVEL
AB This qualitative study investigated factors contributing to the use of the first language (L1) in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classrooms in Jordanian public secondary schools. Using convenience sampling, 25 participants were recruited: four EFL supervisors from an education directorate, 10 EFL teachers, and 11 students from Grades 11 and 12 across multiple public secondary schools. Data were collected through individual semi-structured interviews. Thematic analysis was employed, following open, axial, and selective coding to extract key themes. The findings reveal that L1 use is shaped by a constellation of interrelated factors: teacher-related (e.g. limited L2 proficiency and underuse of listening and speaking activities), student-related (e.g. low L2 proficiency and exam-oriented learning), institutional (e.g. overcrowded classrooms, lack of resources), and systemic (e.g. the high-stakes Tawjihi exam that sidelines communicative competence). A notable policy-practice gap emerged, where supervisors emphasized idealistic expectations for L2 use, while teachers and students described L1 reliance as a pragmatic response to contextual constraints. The findings underscore the need for policy reforms, targeted professional development, and assessment redesign that acknowledge on-the-ground realities and promote meaningful L2 engagement.

TI AIDUA (artificial intelligence device use and acceptance) model to
   assess the acceptance of AI in the learning practices of higher
   education students
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial Intelligence Device Use Acceptance Model; cognitive appraisal
   theory; AI adoption; educational technology; student perceptions;
   anthropomorphism; Artificial Intelligence Device Use Acceptance Model;
   cognitive appraisal theory; AI adoption; educational technology; student
   perceptions; anthropomorphism
ID INFORMATION-TECHNOLOGY; PREDICTION; ADOPTION
AB This study investigates the acceptance and use of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education by applying the Artificial Intelligence Device Acceptance and Use (AIDUA) model, grounded in Lazarus's cognition-motivation-emotion framework. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 220 university students in Ecuador, a developing country with growing access to digital education. Participants had prior experience with technology-based platforms, and Structural Equation Modeling was employed to test the model. Findings indicate that performance expectancy was the strongest driver of positive emotions toward AI, whereas effort expectancy negatively influenced emotions. Emotions significantly predicted both willingness to adopt and objection to AI in academic contexts. Anthropomorphism showed a dual effect, enhancing performance expectancy while also raising perceived effort. Social influence and hedonic motivation positively affected performance expectancy but, contrary to expectations, did not impact effort expectancy. These results highlight the cultural and institutional dynamics of Ecuadorian higher education, where AI is widely used but not necessarily perceived as effortless. The study validates the AIDUA model in a new cultural context and underscores the role of emotional and cognitive mechanisms in shaping AI adoption.

TI Assessing the differentiated learning practice within islamic primary
   schools: challenges in the absence of technology
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Differentiated instruction; technology-enhanced learning; Islamic
   primary schools
ID INSTRUCTION; STRATEGIES; SIZE
AB The concept of learning that accommodates students' learning needs has become a pedagogical concern. In today's classroom, Differentiated Instruction (DI) plays a pivotal role in addressing students' needs. However, DI is a lot of work that needs technology support to implement structurally. This study elaborates on the practice of DI based on Ann Tomlinson's concept and examines the challenges faced by Islamic primary schools in East Java, in implementing DI with a lack of technological support. Adopting a multi-site phenomenological approach, data were collected through data documentation, in-depth interviews and focus group discussions with teachers and principals in five Islamic primary schools in East Java province. Findings revealed that the challenges in implementing DI were inadequate professional trainings in technology-enhanced learnings, a lack of teachers' skill in assessing and identifying students' learning progress, and lack of technological learning resources. Consequently, the practice of DI within Islamic primary schools failed to address students' learning need. This research suggests a practical recommendation for Islamic educational institutions to improve the quality of DI practice through technology-enhanced learning.

TI Investigation of the phonological awareness of A1 level students
   learning Turkish as a foreign language
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Phonological awareness; reading skills; reading skills in foreign
   language education; teaching turkish as a foreign language; components
   of reading
ID SEX-DIFFERENCES
AB Phonological awareness is pivotal in language learning, influencing speaking, writing, and listening abilities. Identifying factors that affect reading development is crucial for effective language instruction. This study explores the phonological awareness of A1-level learners of Turkish as a foreign language (TFL), examining how native language backgrounds impact this foundational skill. Ninety-three participants, whose native languages include Arabic, Indonesian, French, Russian, and Kazakh, were assessed using the Phonological Awareness subtest from the Early Literacy Test (EROT). Data analysis employed non-parametric statistical methods, specifically the Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis tests. Results revealed no statistically significant relationship between gender and phonological awareness, although female participants exhibited higher average scores than males. Among native language groups, Kazakh speakers achieved the highest phonological awareness scores, whereas Indonesian speakers scored the lowest. These findings indicate that a learner's native language significantly influences their phonological awareness in Turkish. Despite its limited scope, this pilot study underscores the essential role of phonological awareness in developing comprehensive language skills in TFL learners. l.

TI Competency-based curriculum in Tanzania: Charting dilemmas for
   successful implementation
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Competency-based curriculum; Tanzania; dilemmas; education; curriculum
   implementation; teacher readiness
AB A competency-based curriculum (CBC) provides learners with the essential skills for the job market and helps them adapt to the modern world's needs. Despite its perceived importance, Tanzania faces multiple challenges that prevent CBC from achieving smooth implementation. Previous research studies have highlighted the need to adopt this paradigm and the related challenges. However, the implementation is still weak, calling for understanding the core dilemmas that prevent its successful implementation. Thus, this study investigated the fundamental dilemmas that affect the implementation of a competency-based curriculum in Njombe Region, Tanzania. A total of 78 participants, including teachers, school administrators, and students, used a qualitative research method involving interviews and focus group discussions to examine the dilemmas constraining the effective implementation of CBC. The research identified multiple core dilemmas related to teachers' readiness, resource distribution, assessment approaches, and societal expectations. The findings showed that many teachers lack adequate training and support to implement CBC, highlighting a gap in professional readiness. Resource distribution is highly uneven, with rural schools facing severe shortages of materials and infrastructure. Assessment practices remain dominated by traditional exams, conflicting with the CBC's emphasis on continuous, skills-based evaluation. Societal expectations still favour academic grades over practical competencies, creating resistance to the curriculum's goals. Effective CBC implementation in Tanzania requires local solutions, continuous teacher training, and collaborative efforts to overcome its challenges. This initiative would help shift from vague descriptions of CBC in Tanzania to identifying key dilemmas in implementation, thus providing nuanced, context-specific insights into why the implementation of the CBC remains low, despite the policy support.

TI Empowering sustainable agriculture education through hydroponic
   literacy: insights from Indonesia's Merdeka Curriculum
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Education; Hydroponic literacy; Merdeka Curriculum; STEM; sustainable
   agriculture; Education; Hydroponic literacy; Merdeka Curriculum; STEM;
   sustainable agriculture
AB With its revolutionary method of teaching sustainable agriculture, hydroponics gives a priceless chance to improve students' comprehension of ecological systems and resource conservation. With a focus on connecting with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and competencies in Indonesia's Merdeka Curriculum, we explore the possibilities of incorporating hydroponic literacy into high school curricula in this article. Students' critical thinking, environmental awareness, and problem-solving abilities may be developed through hydroponic education's emphasis on real-world applications and transdisciplinary learning. This method promotes experiential learning and applying science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) principles in practical settings using easily accessible hydroponic models, such as the Wick system and digital monitoring systems. To guarantee successful curriculum development, we propose incorporating hydroponics into the classroom, necessitating supporting educational policies aligning with the Pancasila Student Profile (P5) criteria. Furthermore, to empower students as future proponents of sustainable agriculture, professional development programs should address issues with resource allocation and teacher preparedness.

TI Exploring students' perceptions of GenAI tools in higher education: a
   case study
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Students' perceptions; GenAI; intelligent learning environments;
   educational technology adoption; higher education; Students'
   perceptions; GenAI; intelligent learning environments; educational
   technology adoption; higher education
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; ADOPTION
AB As artificial intelligence transforms the educational landscape, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools have become influential in enhancing learning experiences. Despite their growing presence in higher education, limited research explores how university students, especially learners in non-Western contexts, perceive these tools. This study investigates students' perceptions at a university in the UAE, focusing on five dimensions: perceived benefits, institutional support, technological self-efficacy, ethical considerations and user satisfaction. The findings reveal that students generally expressed strong agreement regarding the benefits of GenAI, demonstrated a clear sense of ethical awareness and felt confident in their technological abilities. While satisfaction levels were generally high, perceptions of institutional support were more moderate. The study also identified notable differences across academic disciplines, particularly among students in Natural and Health Sciences and Interdisciplinary Studies. These insights contribute to understanding the evolving role of GenAI tools in shaping intelligent learning environments and offer practical recommendations for educators and policymakers seeking to integrate these technologies in higher education.

TI Ethical crisis and educational path for children in the AI era-centred
   on the importance of education for goodness
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Children; Ethical Crisis; Education for Goodness; Humanistic Education;
   Educational Path; Children; Ethical Crisis; Education for Goodness;
   Humanistic Education; Educational Path
AB This paper adopts a child-centered approach to ethical education, employing case studies to examine children's ethical dilemmas and solutions in the age of generative AI. In the Industry 2.0 era, children as 'digital natives' face cognitive challenges in distinguishing between virtual and real-world ethics. The imbalance between technological advancement and ethical education has led to cognitive disorientation and ethical confusion. These crises manifest in four forms: 'children defined by rules, disordered children, children without privacy, and challenged children'. Fundamentally, the crisis reflects AI's reinterpretation of human nature, the consequences of evolutionary laws, and the modern redefinition of traditional 'human-object' relationships. To address this, we propose three strategies: protecting childhood through AI-assisted exploration; integrating classical wisdom to establish human-machine collaboration; promoting human-machine integration while strengthening risk prevention through legislation and moral education. Ultimately, this aims to build a new human-machine ethics framework that achieves 'technology for good'.

TI Dietary education in Japanese and Korean middle schools: contents and
   pedagogical styles from a constructivist perspective
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Constructivist perspective; home economics textbook; dietary education;
   educational content; pedagogical styles; Constructivist perspective;
   home economics textbook; dietary education; educational content;
   pedagogical styles
AB The purpose of this study was to compare home economics textbooks used in Japanese and Korean middle schools from the constructivist perspective to examine whether home economics of both countries can promote constructivist learning. For this, the educational contents of textbooks were analyzed from the constructivist perspective. Pedagogical styles of the texts and exercises were classified into four types: Neutral informative, injunctive, persuasive, and participative. The study data consisted commonly used Japanese textbooks (n = 3) and Korean textbooks (n = 6). Compared to Japanese textbooks, we found that Korean textbooks need contents such as context reflecting historical, cultural, and social situations, which are learning elements from the constructivist perspective. Korean textbooks contained limited dietary problems, and these only related to individuals and families. In both countries, the pedagogical styles were usually participative style in exercises (Japan: 61.5%, Korea: 60.4%), but in texts, the proportion of participative style, reflecting the social constructivist perspective, was low (Japan: 5.7%, Korea: 0.7%). It is recommended that systems be established to support the successful implementation of constructivist learning by providing clearer textbook-writing guidelines tailored to constructivist learning, textbook accreditation standards, and curriculum content that reflects a constructivist perspective in teacher education programs.

ID GENETICS CONCEPTS; DESIGN
AB Although studies have identified numerous confusing concepts in high school biology, existing diagnostic and instructional methods remain inadequate. To address this, we developed a novel 5C teaching method that guides students to clarify concepts through self-directed concept mapping. Eighty-two 10th-grade students from Foshan, China, were randomly assigned to experimental (5C intervention) or control (traditional teaching) groups. A five-tier diagnostic test identified confusing concepts in genetics and cell biology. Results showed that the 5C approach significantly improved students' conceptual clarity and autonomous learning abilities compared to conventional instruction. This method not only enhances conceptual understanding but also promotes critical thinking, collaboration, and learning strategy use, offering a valuable reference for biology educators.

TI 'AIA-PCEK': A new framework for teaching with AI
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AIA-PCEK; TPACK; generative AI; teacher education; ethics; AI literacy;
   critical thinking
ID PEDAGOGICAL CONTENT KNOWLEDGE
AB The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education is reshaping teaching and learning paradigms, transforming AI from a passive tool into an adaptive, autonomous agent capable of complex, human-like interactions. This shift has been accelerated by the emergence of generative AI capable of autonomous behaviors and adaptive learning. While the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework has long guided educators in technology integration, its foundational assumptions about technology as static and teacher-controlled are increasingly lacking flexibility to accommodate the dynamic, interactive nature of AI. This paper introduces AIA-PCEK (Artificial Intelligence Agent - Pedagogical Content Ethical Knowledge), a framework that reconceptualizes teacher knowledge by integrating AI-agent literacy, ethical oversight, adaptive content management, and the cultivation of critical thinking. To support the development of AIA-PCEK, a bibliometric analysis was conducted using major academic databases (Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar), covering literature from 2006 to 2023. These findings were triangulated with qualitative insights from the Erasmus + VOLCANIC project, which trained in-service teachers in AI-enhanced pedagogies. This study positions AIA-PCEK as a comprehensive model that enables educators to address the pedagogical, ethical, and interactive dimensions of AI in classrooms, providing strategies for responsible integration while fostering student autonomy and critical thinking in AI-supported environment.

   teachers
SO COGENT EDUCATION

   basic school teachers; assessment practices; professional development
ID PERCEPTIONS; STANDARDS; EDUCATION; ENGLISH; POLICY
AB This study investigated classroom assessment literacy (CAL) of basic school teachers in Ghana, focusing on understanding their assessment beliefs and practices. Using a quantitative survey design, data were collected from 406 teachers selected through a multistage sampling procedure. Participants responded to the Assessment Literacy Inventory (ALI), and data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and latent profile analysis. Results indicated that the majority of teachers demonstrated a high level of assessment literacy. Enhancing holistic assessment practices requires targeted support that not only builds technical knowledge but also considers teachers' orientations towards assessment.

TI The SASMC effectiveness in improving mathematics learning outcomes and
   students' cultural knowledge
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Improving learning process; classroom activity; cultural ability;
   learning outcome; Education Quality
ID EDUCATION; MODEL; CURRICULUM; QUALITY; IMPACT
AB Learning innovation to improve education is an essential foundation for educational sustainability. Previous studies have demonstrated the potential of culture-based learning to enhance engagement and contextual understanding, yet limited attention has been given to integrating local Malay culture into structured mathematics learning. This study extends prior research by testing the effectiveness of mathematics learning using Student Activity Sheets based on Malay Culture (SASMC) compared with Direct Learning (DL), not only in improving students' mathematical learning outcomes but also in strengthening motivation to learn and preserve Riau Malay culture. The research employed a quantitative quasi-experimental design involving 290 students from five selected schools with two homogeneous classes each. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, t-tests, and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). The results show that SASMC significantly increased learning outcomes (Cohen's d = 0.82, large effect) and motivation to learn Malay culture (Cohen's d = 0.76, large effect) in four schools compared with DL. ANOVA also revealed significant differences in learning outcomes (eta(2) = 0.12) and cultural knowledge (eta(2) = 0.15) across the five schools applying SASMC, indicating meaningful practical impact. The study's limitation is that the quasi-experimental control was constrained due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Nevertheless, the findings provide robust evidence that integrating SASMC expands prior research by offering a sustainable learning model that simultaneously advances mathematics achievement and cultural knowledge. Therefore, applying SASMC is more effective than DL for improving students' academic performance while fostering educational sustainability through cultural preservation.

TI At a heartland of researcher development: 'finding the beat' of human
   and AI-supported technology
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Novice researcher development; qualitative research guides; meta-map;
   ATLAS.ti (TM) & AI; narrative moments; Social Sciences; Education;
   Higher Education; Study of Higher Education; Teaching & Learning
ID INNOVATION
AB This article offers insights for researcher development, specifically to those within novice or advisory roles, to consider key decision 'moments' in research and to have those decisions guided by methodological support for such moments. Consistent with this point of departure, the researcher used a lens of 'narrative moments' to capture building the qualitative research process in its several ways. These narrative moments distil how researchers may use process maps (referred to as a meta-map for this study) accompanied by technological tools, such as ATLAS.ti (TM) with its Artificial Intelligence (AI) functionalities (hereafter, ATLAS.ti), to support the robustness of the methodological audit trail around conventions of the scholarly method. The study relies ethically on the self-narration of these moments drawn from different modes of researcher engagement over ten years of researcher development. The paper contributes to the debates around three issues: how, pragmatically, to make sense of the research process; the merits of a research guide, or not, to respond to the coherence of the research process, and then, the potential for using ATLAS.ti for research conventions, across disciplines, in the undertaking of research. In relation to the latter, the paper surfaces the uses of AI capabilities for research, a burgeoning area that warrants on-going exploration. It also contends that the meta-map and Qualitative Data Analysis Software (QDAS) empower researchers, who might not regularly be able to engage with mainstream researcher development opportunities, to work autonomously on on-going research projects.

   Foreign Language; AI in education; Teaching methodologies
AB The use of virtual games can provide immersive learning experiences. Advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) constitute potential of these games for personalised learning. However, many current virtual games have not integrated AI, limiting their benefits. This study addresses this gap by developing a 3D scenario-based game that leverages generative AI for vocabulary acquisition and conversation practice. This study provides valuable insights into teachers' needs for generative AI-supported 3D scenario-based games, informing their future development.

TI Enhancing intermediate level Afghan EFL learners' reading comprehension
   through the use of jigsaw strategy
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Cooperative learning; jigsaw; EFL learners; reading comprehension;
   perceptions; Social Sciences; Education; Classroom Practice; Assessment
   & Testing; Teaching & Learning
AB Cooperative Learning as a student-centered approach to learning has powerfully influenced language learning since 1970s. The Jigsaw strategy which is one of the widely used cooperative-based instructional methods has been highly effective in improving students' academic performance, particularly in reading comprehension. This study was conducted to find the effect of jigsaw on Afghan EFL learners' reading comprehension and explore their perceptions towards it. The study used one-group pre/post-test experimental design. Participants (N = 20), selected non-randomly, were intermediate EFL learners from a Private Language Learning Institute in Ghazni, Afghanistan. Prior to the study, a pre comprehension test was administered. Students then were engaged in jigsaw activity for eight weeks, and finally sat for a post comprehension test. Comparing the means of two tests, it was found that the jigsaw intervention significantly improved the participants' reading comprehension by the mean difference of 2.20. A paired sample t-test was further conducted, results of which indicated statistically significant difference in participants' performance after engaging in jigsaw as the t-value was quite large (6.18) and the p-value was low (<0.001). In addition, a Cohen's d effect size was calculated to understand the practical significance of the findings. The effect size was very large (1.38), indicating that the improvement was also practically meaningful.

TI Teaching or sensitising? Rwandan teachers' experiences in integrating
   genocide studies across the curriculum
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Rwandan teachers' experiences; integrating genocide studies across the
   curriculum; teaching or sensitising; Arts & Humanities; Arts; Music;
   Music & Education; Teaching Performance; Social Sciences; Education;
   Genocide Studies
AB The purpose of this study was to analyse teachers' thoughts in integrating genocide studies into their disciplines as a cross-cutting issue. It is assumed that this integration provides learners with several opportunities, including gaining knowledge about the genocide against the Tutsi, its progression, effects and prevention mechanisms. Other general skills, such as critical thinking and comparing different genocides, are also included in the curriculum. Several publications focus on the genocide as a historical event and on how to teach and learn about this tragic event. However, little is known about how genocide studies are incorporated across various subjects in Rwandan secondary schools. Through a qualitative career life story using document analysis and semi-structured interviews with 23 science, humanities and language teachers purposively selected from three provinces. This study shows that all teachers, without exception, are aware of the definition of genocide. They have different views on the integration of genocide studies across subjects. The integration is often done through improvisation; some science teachers begin discussions related to the genocide against the Tutsi to educate against it. Due to the topic's sensitivity, teachers often prefer to use a lecture-based approach to present a widely accepted version, which can be shared both inside and outside the school. To overcome these challenges, integrating genocide studies into teaching and learning requires reevaluating teaching methods, enhancing teacher competence and ensuring resource availability. The study recommends training to all teachers on Rwanda's history to improve their understanding of the genocide. Moreover, an interdisciplinary, whole-school approach through team teaching should be developed, supported by both physical and digital teaching resources. This approach can motivate teachers and students alike, leading to a deeper and more comprehensive understanding of genocide studies.

ID CONTENT KNOWLEDGE; PRESERVICE; ACHIEVEMENT; EDUCATION; EFFICACY; INQUIRY
AB Pedagogical understanding is an issue that has existed for a long time and is still a focus of attention for the Indonesian government. The purpose of this study is to (1) explore and describe the extent to which prospective elementary school teacher students understand the concept of science pedagogy based on their educational background, and (2) explore ways to develop students' pedagogical understanding. The study used a descriptive qualitative method, involving six lecturers and 130 students through purposive sampling. Data were collected through semi-structured in-depth interviews, documentation, and questionnaires as well as the use of thematic analysis by Braun and Clarke. This study shows that students' understanding of science pedagogy is reflected in two main themes: (1) conditions of pedagogical ability (e.g. mastery of student characteristics, science learning theory, and curriculum development) and (2) opportunities for development through education and training. Thematic analysis revealed significant gaps, particularly in mastery of science learning theory (23.6%), highlighting the need for targeted training in inquiry-based and experimental approaches for Indonesian teacher education programs. These findings urge Indonesian teacher training programs to integrate more field practice and contextual pedagogical strategies. PUBLIC INTEREST STATEMENT This study reveals that most future elementary teachers in Indonesia struggle to teach science effectively, even those with science backgrounds. It calls for urgent reforms in teacher training to prioritize hands-on, inquiry-based methods critical for nurturing young learners' curiosity in STEM fields. The findings are relevant to educators and policymakers in similar global contexts where science education faces challenges.

TI The effect of transformational leadership on teachers' Organizational
   Citizenship Behavior in Amhara Regional State public universities,
   Ethiopia
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Transformational leadership; organizational citizenship behavior;
   idealized influence; inspirational motivation; individualized
   consideration
ID JOB-SATISFACTION; IMPACT; SUGGESTIONS; PERFORMANCE; SCHOOLS
AB This study explored the practice of transformational leadership (TL) among university leaders and its impact on teachers' organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) in Ethiopian public universities in the Amhara region. A quantitative, cross-sectional survey was conducted with 647 respondents, and data were analyzed using t-tests, correlation analysis, multiple regression, and structural equation modeling. Results indicated that TL was moderately practiced and had a significant but modest correlation with OCB. Among TL components, idealized influence had the strongest effect, followed by inspirational motivation, while intellectual stimulation and individualized consideration were not significant predictors. The structural model confirmed TL's direct effect on OCB. The study recommends leadership development programs to strengthen key TL dimensions that foster OCB. Future research should examine contextual factors limiting the impact of some TL components to enhance leadership strategies that improve teachers' OCB and institutional performance.

   contemporary chemical engineering curriculum
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article

ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; REALITY; PROPOSAL; SCIENCE
AB This paper discusses how artificial intelligence and machine learning can be incorporated into the new curricula of chemical engineering education as part of the transformation facing the challenges of Industry 4.0. It describes the ways in which AI tools, adaptive learning platforms, virtual laboratories, intelligent tutoring systems, and automatic assessments can significantly improve teaching effectiveness, resulting in corresponding increases in student learning outcomes. TI Teachers' wellbeing at work: a Finnish survey study on teachers' work
   experiences
SO COGENT EDUCATION

DT Article
DE Teacher; work experience; salutogenic factors; sense of coherence; WEMS
ID ILLEGITIMATE TASKS; FAMILY CONFLICT; ENGAGEMENT; SATISFACTION;
   RESOURCES; BURNOUT; QUALITY; STRESS; REFORM; MODEL
AB This study explores the working life experiences of teachers, adopting a salutogenic perspective emphasising positive health, wellbeing and health promotion principles. An electronic survey was sent out to members of a trade union for teachers in spring 2020. More than 1,300 teachers responded to the survey, including the Work Experience Measurement Scale (WEMS) instrument, which contains six dimensions of work experience: supportive work conditions, internal work experiences, autonomy, time experience, leadership and process of change. Correlation and regression analyses were conducted to examine the relationships between the variables Age, Workplace, Gender and the six dimensions of WEMS, plus the WEMS total. Teachers working at comprehensive school grades 7-9 had significantly lower ratings in the WEMS total than teachers in other workplace groups. Older age predicted lower ratings in the aspect of Process of Change. Teachers, altogether, evaluate their work experiences as reasonably good. Time experience is the most challenging dimension in teachers' working life.

TI Strengthening the foundation: the role of supervision in improving
   quality service provision in pre-primary education of Gambella Regional
   State, Ethiopia
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pre-primary education; quality service provision; role of supervision;
   strengthening the foundation; Gambella Regional State; Ethiopia; Early
   Childhood; Classroom Practice; Early Years
AB Pre-primary education is critical for children's cognitive, social and emotional development, forming the foundation for academic success. Grounded in Contingency Theory, which emphasizes the importance of aligning organizational structures and processes with the specific context and needs of the organization, this study investigates the role of supervision in quality service provision in pre-primary schools in Gambella Regional State, Ethiopia. Employing a convergent mixed-methods design, the study involved a census sample of 190 teachers and 95 principals from all pre-primary schools in four selected woredas. Qualitative data were collected through interviews with five education experts from the Regional Education Bureau, three from the zonal education department, and eight Parent-Teacher Association leaders, as well as four focus group discussions (FGDs) with 28 education experts from woreda education offices. The analysis revealed significant gaps in the quality of service provision and supervision practices. Effective supervision is essential for enhancing the physical learning environment, teacher-learner interactions, addressing diverse student needs, supporting play-based learning and fostering professional development. Inferential statistics, including correlation and linear regression analyses, were employed to assess the influence of supervision on quality service provision. The results indicate positive correlation (r = 0.250, p < 0.001) between supervision and quality service provision, with about 6.3% of the variability in quality being explained by supervision practices. This study contributes to the literature on pre-primary education in Ethiopia, highlighting the need for targeted interventions to enhance supervision and curriculum implementation. IMPACT STATEMENT The study underscores the critical role of effective supervision in improving the qualityof pre-primary education in Gambella, leading to better educational outcomes for children.

TI Enhancing concept mapping skills through load reduction instruction in
   an academic English course: a mixed methods study
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Cognitive load theory; load reduction instruction; concept mapping;
   student-generated concept maps; concept map quality; Social Sciences;
   Education; Curriculum; Language Pedagogy
ID STUDENTS LEARNING ACHIEVEMENTS; COGNITIVE ARCHITECTURE; DESIGN
AB Concept mapping is an effective reading strategy that enhances students' understanding of complex subjects and fosters meaningful learning. However, this technique remains underutilized due to cognitive challenges and insufficient training. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) and the Load Reduction Instruction (LRI) framework, this study developed and evaluated a concept mapping training program using a mixed methods approach. Sixty-nine university students enrolled in an Academic English course participated in the study. Results indicate that the experimental group who received the training achieved significantly higher concept map scores, experienced lower intrinsic and extraneous cognitive loads, and reported increased germane cognitive load compared to the control group. Multiple regression analysis revealed that germane cognitive load was a significant positive predictor of concept map quality. Semi-structured interviews corroborated these findings, providing insights into students' positive experiences with the training program. The results demonstrate the efficacy of our LRI-based training program in addressing cognitive load challenges and offer educators a structured pedagogical framework to guide students from novice to proficient concept mappers.

TI Ethnic minority students' attitudes and experiences with Mobile English
   Learning Resources in Qinghai: an activity theory analysis
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Mobile English Learning Resources (MELRs); ethnic minority students;
   activity theory (AT); reflexive thematic analysis (RTA); Qinghai; Social
   Sciences; Development Studies, Environment, Social Work, Urban Studies;
   Education; Educational Technology; Teacher Education and Training;
   Education and Training
ID EDUCATION; VOCABULARY; UNIVERSITY; SCHOOLS; POLICY; ICT
AB This qualitative study explores how ethnic minority university students in Qinghai, China, engage with Mobile English Learning Resources (MELRs) amid linguistic, cultural, and institutional constraints. Guided by Activity Theory (AT) and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis (RTA), the study drew on interviews and reflective journals. The participants were eight first-year non-English-major undergraduates, all Tibetan L1 speakers, from Tibetan, Mongolian, and Tu ethnic backgrounds. Two interconnected themes were developed: Empowerment within Frustration and Unequal Foundations and Missing Scaffolds. While students appreciated the flexibility and authentic exposure offered by MELRs, their engagement was often constrained by curriculum misalignment, limited digital experience, and a lack of sustained instructional and peer support. Through the lens of AT, the study identified four secondary contradictions within the activity system: between tools and subjects, rules and tools, community and tools, and division of labour and tools. Rather than attributing difficulties to individual shortcomings, the findings foreground systemic tensions shaping mobile learning experiences. The study highlights the importance of responsive, scaffolded, and contextually aligned mobile learning practices in supporting students from multilingual and under-resourced regions.

TI Integrating automatic speech recognition and automated writing
   evaluation to reduce speaking anxiety and enhance speaking competence
   among Chinese EFL learners
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Automatic speech recognition (ASR); automated writing evaluation (AWE);
   speaking anxiety; speaking competence; technology-enhanced language
   learning
ID LANGUAGE; ACCEPTANCE
AB This study investigates how the combined use of automatic speech recognition (ASR) and automated writing evaluation (AWE) influences Chinese English as a foreign language (EFL) learners' speaking anxiety and speaking performance. Adopting a mixed-methods experimental design, the study compares an experimental group (EG) that utilizes ASR-AWE tools with a control group (CG) that follows traditional speaking instruction. The results revealed significant reductions in speaking anxiety, especially in learners with low self-confidence, fear of making mistakes and fear of being laughed at. In terms of competence, the EG demonstrated statistically significant improvements in pronunciation, grammatical accuracy and interactive communication. Qualitative findings indicated that learners valued ASR for its real-time feedback on pronunciation and AWE for improving sentence structure and grammatical refinement. The integration of ASR and AWE supported autonomous, iterative speaking practice, providing targeted linguistic input and facilitating learner engagement. These findings offer practical implications for incorporating ASR-AWE technologies into oral communication curricula in EFL contexts, particularly in promoting student confidence and fluency in technology-supported environments.

TI Unraveling the nexus between learning styles and academic performance:
   the mediating effect of pre-service teachers' satisfaction
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic performance; colleges of education; learning styles;
   pre-service teachers; student satisfaction; Academic performance;
   colleges of education; learning styles; pre-service teachers; student
   satisfaction
ID STUDENT SATISFACTION
AB Effective teaching is shaped not only by what pre-service teachers know, but also by how they learn during their training and the attitudes they develop towards their own learning. This study examined the mediating effect of pre-service teachers' satisfaction in the relationship between Grasha-Reichmann learning styles and academic performance. Participants for the study were selected from Colleges of Education located in the Ashanti region of Ghana. Employing a descriptive research design, 291 pre-service teachers were sampled through multistage sampling. However, 287 (98.6%) participant responses were deemed accurate and used for the analysis. The analysis revealed direct significant effects of five learning styles (collaborative, dependent, independent, avoidant, and participant) on academic performance, while the competitive style showed no direct effect. However, when mediated by students' satisfaction, all six learning styles, including competitive, exhibited significant indirect effects on academic performance. These findings highlight the critical role of addressing diverse learning preferences and nurturing students' satisfaction to enhance pre-service teachers' preparedness. Educators at the Colleges of Education should prioritise strategies that integrate these insights, fostering holistic development for future teaching professionals.

TI Perceptions, pitfalls, and proposals for the ethical use of artificial
   intelligence in the classroom: a case study of students and educators
   (teachers' and lecturers')
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; ethical use; perceptions; pitfalls; Classroom;
   students and educators; Social Sciences; Education; Classroom Practice;
   Assessment & Testing; Teaching & Learning
AB Regarding the use and effects of artificial intelligence (AI) in Tanzanian educational settings, this study investigated the opinions and experiences of important education stakeholders, such as students, teachers, and lecturers. The study used a mixed-methods (quantitative and qualitative), guided by the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework, Theory of Planned Behaviour, and Stakeholder Theory. Interviews and questionnaires were used to collect information from 59 people. Although a vast majority of the participants (91.4%) had either used or encountered AI being utilised in learning, in programs like ChatGPT and Grammarly, the results revealed that opinions still differ greatly. While teachers and lecturers fear decreased cognitive engagement, copying, and ethical misuse, learners typically see AI as a tool that improves learning and academic performance. Interestingly, more than 80% of learners said that using AI had enhanced their schooling achievement; nevertheless, over 50% of teachers felt that pupils did not fully understand the work that AI generated. In addition, 70.7% of the participants agreed that the usage of AI promotes academic dishonesty and reduces critical thinking. These results indicate the pressing need for rules of ethics, digital literacy instruction, and institutional norms that encourage the ethical and pedagogically sound use of AI in education. In the end, the study offers substantial new data to guide practices and regulations that match the integration of AI with competency-based, inclusive, and ethical instruction in the age of technology.

TI Developing a new course guided by students' perceived motivational
   climate. Insights from higher education in Iceland
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Communication in health care; course development; higher education;
   motivation; the MUSIC Model; student feedback; teaching methods;
   Communication in health care; course development; higher education;
   motivation; the MUSIC Model; student feedback; teaching methods
AB This mixed methods study aimed to employ students' perceptions of motivational factors and attained learning goals in developing and improving a nursing course in communication in health care and patient education. Data was collected from two consecutive cohorts of students (N = 144) using the MUSIC (R) Model of Motivation Inventory, which measures factors, namely eMpowerment, Usefulness, Success, Interest, and Caring, that, when present, motivate students to engage in their studies. The survey also included five items regarding students' belief in their possibilities of developing problem-solving and critical thinking skills in the course. A focus group that was conducted after the first cohort responded to the survey provided a deeper understanding of the results. This information aided in further course development. In the subsequent survey, the second cohort had a statistically higher score for three of the five motivation factors (U, S, and I, p < 0.01) than the first cohort, as well as a higher interest score for appreciation of teaching methods (p < 0.05). Students' belief in attaining learning goals, such as problem-solving skills, was also statistically higher for the second cohort (p < 0.05). We recommend using the MUSIC Inventory to gain students' feedback to develop or improve courses.

TI A qualitative investigation into the factors influencing
   underrepresentation and performance of black STEM female learners in a
   South African public secondary school
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE STEM; Black; women; underperformance; underrepresentation; secondary
   school; South Africa
ID GENDER STEREOTYPES; INTERSECTIONALITY
AB Despite reforms in the education system and the availability of financial support and mentorship, women remain underrepresented in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) fields. This study applied intersectionality to examine factors contributing to the underrepresentation of young women in STEM in the Further Education and Training (FET) phase in a South African public school. Intersectionality highlights how multiple forms of oppression intersect to shape the experiences of marginalised groups. A descriptive qualitative design was adopted, focusing on black female learners aged 15-18. Participants were recruited through snowball sampling technique, and data were collected through one-on-one telephonic interviews. Thematic analysis was used to interpret the data. Findings revealed that most participants doubted their technical abilities to succeed in STEM. Many had internalised gender stereotypes that positioned them in nurturing roles rather than technical fields. The school environment was under-resourced, further constraining their studies. In addition, socioeconomic challenges such as inadequate housing and loadshedding disrupted learning after school hours. The study concludes that government should prioritise investment in public school infrastructure and provide mentorship opportunities for underprivileged female learners in STEM fields.

TI Development and early reach of a podcast-based innovation to support
   medical residents' personal and professional development
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Podcast; resident well-being; resident support; educational innovation;
   stress management in residency; work-life balance
AB Despite the use of structured competency frameworks and supporting educational tools, medical residents often continue to struggle with personalising their learning, managing feedback, and balancing professional demands with personal well-being. These persistent challenges suggest that conventional support systems may not fully address the nuanced needs of residents, contributing to feelings of disconnection and stress during training. The Resident Talks Podcast was developed to provide residents with accessible insights and practical tools to support their personal and professional development, particularly in areas such as work-life balance, stress management, and feedback integration. The podcast was developed in the Netherlands by a research group studying EPA-based residency training. It was inspired by insights from their qualitative studies and shaped in collaboration with residents. Social media engagement ensured the content remained relevant to their evolving needs. Topics ranged from professional identity, feedback culture and mental health to more sensitive or underrepresented issues such as pregnancy, diversity and addiction. Each 30-minute episode was distributed across platforms like Spotify and Apple Podcasts to maximise accessibility. To date, the podcast has released 21 episodes and garnered over 14,700 downloads. Feedback highlights its practical value and relevance in addressing issues that are not always openly discussed in formal training. The Resident Talks Podcast demonstrates the potential of innovative media to supplement resident support systems, addressing personal and professional challenges in a flexible and accessible way. Further research is needed to evaluate whether and how this format provides meaningful support in daily residency practice.

TI Navigating AI integration in higher education: assessing the impact of
   assessment formats and motivation types on students' AI usage intentions
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Group assessment; individual assessment; controlled motivation;
   autonomous motivation; artificial intelligence; Social Sciences;
   Education; Development Studies, Environment, Social Work, Urban Studies;
   Criminology and Criminal Justice
ID TECHNOLOGY ACCEPTANCE MODEL; AUTONOMOUS MOTIVATION; ACHIEVEMENT GOALS;
   PURSUIT; BIAS
AB Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping teaching and learning, prompting renewed policy attention within higher education. While prior research has explored the antecedents of students' AI usage intentions, limited attention has been given to how these intentions are shaped by assessment formats and motivational orientations. This study investigates how group-based versus individual-based assessments affect students' intentions to use AI-specifically ChatGPT-for learning and exams, considering autonomous and controlled motivations. Survey data from 193 undergraduate and postgraduate business students were analyzed using co-variance-based structural equation modelling techniques. The findings reveal that group-based assessments increase students' likelihood of using AI for learning. While neither autonomous nor controlled motivation directly encourages AI use for learning, controlled motivation reduces AI usage. Notably, autonomous motivation positively moderates the relationship between individual-based assessment and AI use for learning. Finally, students' intention to use AI for learning translates into its use for exams. Implications of these findings for academic institutions, educators and students are discussed.

   competencies
SO COGENT EDUCATION

   sciences; Education; Higher education; Study of higher education;
   Teaching and learning
ID ACADEMIC-PERFORMANCE; UNIVERSITY; STUDENTS; FACULTY
AB Integral mentoring refers to the process by which an expert mentor accompanies the student in the harmonious growth of all their dimensions through the development of personal competencies. Competencies such as personal knowledge and acceptance, search for meaning in life, proactivity, self-management and achievement orientation. This research seeks to contribute theoretically and empirically to the debate on the concept of mentoring and its effectiveness in developing personal competencies by offering results from the application of an integral mentoring program in a Spanish university. A reliable and valid questionnaire on competencies was used as a measurement instrument. The results show significant differences in the level of acquisition of intrapersonal competencies in favor of the university students who received the integral mentoring program. This article also proposes best practices for the design of integral mentoring programs.

TI AI in education and cultural barriers: a mixed-methods study with
   Argentinean university students
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence in education; perceptions; higher education;
   educational Equity; university students; Artificial intelligence in
   education; perceptions; higher education; educational Equity; university
   students
AB This study explore students' use and perceptions of AIEd in Buenos Aires, Argentina, through a large-scale mixed-methods design. Also, associate AIEd perceptions and use with sociodemographic variables, to evaluate possible sociocultural barriers to access. 1033 students from different Argentinean universities (M.age= 26.95, SD = 9.20, female = 713) completed virtual sociodemographic and the use and perception of AIEd questionnaires. Then, two focus groups (total.n = 47) were applied to deepen the analysis of the perception of barriers and advantages of using AIEd. TI Using music for other subjects in primary schools: empirical survey
   findings from teachers and a systematic scoping review
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Musicality; musical instruments; singing; song; elementary school;
   courses; pseudo-replicates; Arts and Humanities; Arts; Music; Music and
   Education; Music in Primary Education
AB Teachers implement music for other subjects, mostly based on intuition. We studied the added value of music for other subjects within primary school settings, with a single-school survey and a scoping literature review. Our paper-based survey of 14 Dutch primary school teachers shows that they intuitively use music for teaching content in other subjects, mainly for language learning. These teachers see potential for increased use. This survey is the first to identify teachers' perceived need for further training and materials for this (workshops, other types of training, and the availability of integrated teaching methods). Our scoping review included 49 scientific publications describing the use of music, either as a supplementary teaching tool or as background music, for other subjects in primary school settings. It confirms music being used for other subjects, mainly languages, mathematics, and gym. Our meta-analysis is the first evidence synthesis to suggest an overall positive effect. However, the risk of bias and heterogeneity were high. Besides our methods and results, we present a convenient list of items to assess the risk of bias in educational studies.

TI Empowering sexuality education: active learning through
   university-school-health-community partnerships
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Health & Society; Nursing; HIV/AIDs; Teachers & Teacher Education;
   Higher Education; Secondary Education; Development Studies, Environment,
   Social Work, Urban Studies; Sustainability Education, Training &
   Leadership; Teachers & Teacher Education; Higher Education; Secondary
   Education; Development Studies, Environment, Social Work, Urban Studies;
   Sustainability Education, Training & Leadership
ID PROGRAM; SEX
AB This quasi-experimental study aimed to determine whether a sexuality education intervention, developed through a university-school-health-community collaboration, effectively improved students' knowledge, attitudes and behaviours regarding sexual health. Utilising project-based and service-based learning, the programme engaged 454 students aged between 13 and 48 years (M = 19.33, SD = 6.03). The quasi-experimental group comprised students from secondary school, a nursing degree and a master's in teaching, while the control group included students from secondary school and bachelors' and masters' degree students in health and education. It fostered trans-inclusive behaviours, promoted positive attitudes towards sexual diversity and reduced sexist beliefs and rape-supportive attitudes. These results highlight the intervention's effectiveness among the participants.

TI Cultural transformation: religious moderation from manuscripts heritage
   to living tradition in Indonesia and Malaysia
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Social Sciences; Education; Social Sciences; Education Policy; Education
   Policy; Pedagogy; Pedagogy; Pedagogy; Pedagogy; Pedagogy; Education
   Policy & Politics; Education Policy & Politics; Education Policy &
   Politics; Education Policy & Politics; Education Policy & Politics;
   Education Policy & Politics; Education Policy & Politics; Education
   Policy & Politics; Education Policy; Humanities; Humanities; Philosophy;
   Philosophy; Philosophy; Philosophy; Philosophy; Arts & Humanities; Arts
   & Humanities; Arts & Humanities; Arts & Humanities; Arts & Humanities;
   Arts & Humanities; Arts & Humanities; Arts & Humanities; Phenomenology;
   Phenomenology; Religion; Religion; Phenomenology; Religion
ID ISLAMIC MANUSCRIPTS
AB This study investigates the role of Islamic manuscripts in Indonesia and Malaysia in fostering religious moderation amid ongoing cultural transformation. These classical texts function not only as sources of Islamic teaching but also as dynamic tools that facilitate the contextual adaptation of Islamic values within diverse local cultures. Employing a qualitative approach-combining philological analysis, in-depth interviews, participant observation (at Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia and in Denpasar, Bali), and digital ethnography through YouTube content-this research highlights the active role of manuscript traditions in shaping peaceful, inclusive, and culturally rooted expressions of moderate Islam. These values are embedded both in the textual contents and in their internalization within communal practices. The study identifies key cases such as gender-equitable inheritance customs, dialogues between local rulers and Islamic scholars, and the gradual Islamization of adat law, particularly in South Sulawesi's Wajo region. These cases demonstrate how Islamic teachings were historically adapted through respectful dialogue, not rigid legalism. Furthermore, the use of Malay as the lingua franca of Islamic scholarship enabled broader integration across a multicultural region. This living tradition, transmitted through both written and oral means-including digital platforms like YouTube-continues to evolve, sustaining the relevance of Islam in diverse local contexts.

TI The impact of human capital on employment quality: a scoping review
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Human capital; employment quality; scoping review; PRISMA-ScR;
   quantitative analysis; vocational training
AB With accelerated globalization and technological advancement, the labor market is undergoing profound transformations, necessitating increasingly advanced skills and knowledge from workers. Human capital refers to productive resources developed through individuals' education, training, experience, and skill acquisition, which significantly enhance a worker's value and productivity in the labor market. Employment quality is an important indicator of workers' employment status. This study aims to examine the impact of human capital on employment quality and clarify the measurement dimensions and elements of both. This study adopts a scoping review methodology based on Arksey & O'Malley's study, five-stage framework, with analysis following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Data were retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science (WoS), and ERIC; ultimately, 30 studies meeting the inclusion criteria were selected for analysis. Existing literature primarily explores the relationship between human capital and employment quality, but comprehensive reviews in this field remain limited. This scoping review systematically synthesizes relevant studies from the past five years to address theoretical and empirical gaps, examining dimensions of human capital and employment quality, target group diversity, and geographic regions. It deepens understanding of their relationship and provides targeted practical insights for policymakers, educators, and employers.

AB This study examines the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools on the academic research output of undergraduate students from a Business School in Peru during 2024. TI Estimating the optimum number of attempts for any university
   examination: a negative binomial approach
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE University examinations; Examination Attempts; Negative Binomial;
   Institutions of Higher Learning; Makerere University
AB This study sought to provide an empirical answer to the question of how many attempts should be allowed to sit for a given University module. We analyzed data from Makerere University, spanning five admissions from 2007 to 2011, for 14 selected modules. We modeled the number of attempts students made on examinations as a count variable using the negative binomial distribution within a Bayesian framework. Our results indicate that while there are differences in the number of attempts across student and academic-specific factors, the number of attempts generally does not exceed three. The study concludes that, given the main objective of university education-to produce well-prepared and competitive graduates, a policy of a maximum of three attempts appears to be reasonable and prudent since it balances the need for student success while maintaining academic rigor.

DT Article

AB This experimental study addressed the critical gap in phonics instruction within under-resourced Pakistani public primary schools, investigating how Technology-Enhanced Language Learning (TELL) tools impact phonics acquisition among students of different ages and gender, to reflect patterns of interest development. Using an action research design with an explanatory sequential mixed-methods approach, 329 Grade 3 (age 9-12) and Grade 5 (age 9-13) learners were divided into control and experimental (TELL-based intervention) groups. Interest development evolved from situational to individual, driven by engaging multimedia content. Implications include urgent integration of TELL tools into pedagogy, tailored teacher training in systematic synthetic phonics, and policy reforms for resource allocation and phonics-focused assessments. Recommendations emphasize the development of localized digital content, sustained professional development, and the integration of interest-driven TELL strategies to enhance foundational literacy in low-resource settings.

TI Student utilization and perceptions of AI technology for academic
   purposes: a mixed-method analysis
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence (AI); digital literacy; higher education;
   mixed-methods research; technology adoption; UTAUT
ID ADOPTION; ACCEPTANCE
AB Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in higher education, yet limited research explores how students in developing countries respond to these technologies. This study investigates the behavioral intentions of university students in Indonesia toward AI-based academic tools using a mixed-methods approach. A quantitative survey was conducted with 388 students across public and private universities, followed by in-depth interviews with 10 selected participants. The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) was used to analyze cognitive factors, while qualitative data explored emotional trust, ethical concerns and institutional support. Findings indicate: Performance expectancy and effort expectancy significantly influence students' attitudes toward AI. Attitude strongly predicts behavioral intention, which in turn leads to actual adoption. Perceived risk, such as concerns about accuracy and plagiarism, was acknowledged but did not significantly impact attitude. Students adopt AI tools strategically, often validating outputs through textbooks or peer input. Institutional support and faculty guidance influence adoption, but formal policies are often unclear. The results suggest that while students recognize the limitations of AI, they prioritize its practical benefits. This study contributes to a more complete understanding of AI use in academic settings and offers actionable recommendations for educators and decision-makers in similar educational systems.

TI Analysis of the subareas of education in universities of a developing
   country: from a multivariate perspective
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Higher education; educational technology; inclusive education; science
   and mathematics education; health and wellness education
ID EMPIRICAL-ANALYSIS
AB This study focuses on an analysis of scientific production in the field of education within universities in developing countries. For this purpose, academic articles were classified into 17 predefined subareas: Higher Education, Educational Technology, Educational Policy, Inclusive Education, Pedagogy and Didactics, Science Education, and Mathematics. A keyword analysis algorithm was designed to identify and classify publications in these subareas using key terms present in the titles, abstracts, and authors' keywords. This study used the multivariate HJ-Biplot technique to visualize the relationship between Ecuadorian universities and the research sub-areas in which they concentrated their scientific production. The results indicated that both public and private universities focus their research on key areas, such as Higher Education, Science and Mathematics Education, Educational Technology, and Inclusive Education, with significant differences in the correlations between subareas. In particular, private universities show a strong correlation between Educational Technology and Health and Wellness Education, whereas the correlation between Inclusive Education and Science and Mathematics Education is weak. Additionally, low representation was identified in emerging sub-areas, such as Educational Policy and Neuroeducation, underscoring the need to foster more research in these areas.

TI The impact of intrapreneurial self-capital on critical thinking and
   academic engagement among Chinese university students
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Intrapreneurial self-capital; critical thinking; academic engagement;
   Chinese university students; structural equation modeling; Social
   Sciences; Education; Higher Education; Study of Higher Education;
   Teaching and Learning
AB University students in China face increasing academic demands and pressures, which makes the development of psychological resources, such as resilience, adaptability, and higher-order thinking essential for their success. This study investigates the relationships between Intrapreneurial Self-Capital (ISC), critical thinking dimensions (open-mindedness, systematicity-analyticity, and truth-seeking), and academic engagement among Chinese university students. Using structural equation modeling with partial least squares (PLS-SEM), we assessed the direct effects of ISC on critical thinking and academic engagement, as well as the mediating role of critical thinking dimensions. Data were collected in two waves from a sample of 1043 students, with ISC measured in the first wave and critical thinking and engagement assessed in the second. Results indicate that ISC significantly predicts both critical thinking and academic engagement, and that systematicity-analyticity and truth-seeking mediate this relationship. These findings highlight the central role of critical thinking dispositions in linking psychological resources to students' academic engagement. Practically, the results suggest that educational practitioners and policymakers could design teaching interventions and training programs that explicitly strengthen ISC and critical thinking to foster deeper academic involvement. The study's quasi-longitudinal design, reliance on self-report data, and overrepresentation of urban students are noted as limitations.

TI How does academic stress affect academic learning? The mediating role of
   internet addiction and the role of alexithymia
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Students; academic stress; academic learning; Internet addiction;
   alexithymia; Educational Psychology; Multidisciplinary Psychology;
   Psychological Science
ID STUDENT ENGAGEMENT; PERCEIVED STRESS; COLLEGE-STUDENTS; PERFORMANCE;
   ASSOCIATION; ANXIETY; MODEL; ADOLESCENTS; ACHIEVEMENT; PERSONALITY
AB Building on the stress-coping model and the alexithymia-stress hypothesis, the present cross-sectional study examined the link between academic stress and a specific facet of academic engagement, i.e. academic learning. More specifically, we examined how academic stress might lead to lower academic learning through Internet addiction symptoms, assuming that Internet addiction would be a coping mechanism used primarily by students with high alexithymia. The convenience sample comprised 301 Romanian university students aged 18 to 25 (M = 20.71, SD = 1.31, 88.4% females). Results suggested that high levels of academic stress were associated with high levels of academic learning. Internet addiction partially mediated the effect of academic stress on academic learning, shaping a significant suppressor effect: higher academic stress, mediated by Internet addiction, was associated with lower academic learning. Also, alexithymia moderated the relationship between academic stress and Internet addiction: high and medium levels of alexithymia significantly increased the influence of academic distress on Internet addiction. We discuss the present findings regarding their implications for students' mental health and educational outcomes.

TI Predictors of psychological well-being among academic staff in malaysian
   higher education: the role of emotional intelligence, self-compassion,
   psychological capital, and mindfulness
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Emotional intelligence; self-compassion; psychological well-being;
   mindfulness; psychological capital; Emotional intelligence;
   self-compassion; psychological well-being; mindfulness; psychological
   capital
AB As higher education institutions respond to both internal and external expectations for sustainable higher education performance, mental health concerns among academic staff with demanding workloads have been given scholarly focus. Therefore, this study aims to examine the effect of self-compassion, emotional intelligence, psychological capital, mindfulness, and psychological well-being among academic staff in Malaysian public research universities. A total of 234 sets of data were collected from academic staff in five Malaysian public research universities using stratified and simple random sampling. The hypotheses were analyzed using Partial Least Squares-Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). The findings evidenced that self-compassion and emotional intelligence positively affect psychological capital. Similarly, psychological capital positively affects psychological well-being. Further, psychological capital mediates the relationship between self-compassion, emotional intelligence, and psychological well-being has been confirmed. However, mindfulness does not significantly moderate the relationship between psychological capital and psychological well-being. The findings contribute to a better understanding of psychological well-being by highlighting the importance of personal resources in the context of higher education settings. Furthermore, this study offers several implications for higher education institutions, the government, and policymakers, who can implement multiple psychological resources development programmes and coping strategies to cultivate their personal resources, thereby contributing to a more inclusive higher education landscape.
